# Compounding Pressures and Scaling Limits {#sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales}

::: {.epigraph}
> "[F]eedback is a method of controlling a system by reinserting into it the results of its past performance. If these results are merely used as numerical data for the criticism of the system and its regulation, we have the simple feedback of the control engineers."
>
> — Norbert Wiener, *The Human Use of Human Beings*, revised edition [@Wiener1989HumanUse, p. 61]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Why has system and chip design become harder to carry through, and where might AI assistance be useful?*

**Core thesis:** *Compounding pressures across physical scaling, specialization, software co-evolution, and verification demand new abstractions, but assistance succeeds only where evaluation costs can be amortized.*
:::

The promise of AI in computer architecture is not an abstract algorithmic luxury; it is born from an urgent engineering crisis. For decades, architects rode the compounding physical dividends of Dennard scaling and Moore's Law: shrinking transistor dimensions reliably boosted switching speeds while keeping power density flat. Today, that combined dividend has largely run out. Subthreshold leakage has stalled supply-voltage scaling, wire resistance limits how far a signal can travel in one cycle, and power budgets leave substantial fractions of a die unable to switch at full frequency at the same time, a condition known as dark silicon. The architectural frontier has consequently shifted from general-purpose scaling to aggressive, domain-specific specialization: heterogeneous accelerator arrays, deep memory hierarchies, and co-designed software runtimes. Specialization also multiplies the coupled, nonlinear trade-offs a team must evaluate, and the number of alternatives worth comparing can grow faster than the tools and engineers available to compare them.

This chapter dissects the physical, microarchitectural, and economic forces driving this architectural crisis. It traces the causal chain from quantum tunneling and interconnect resistance-capacitance (RC) bottlenecks to dark silicon, accelerator offload overheads, and the combinatorial explosion of hardware–software verification. Through concrete engineering analyses, it distinguishes vast design spaces from computationally tractable evaluation loops, demonstrating why machine-assisted exploration succeeds only when targeted at the exact bottleneck delaying an architectural decision (@fig-ch02-cover-map).

![**Compounding pressures shift the architectural bottleneck.** Fading automatic technology gains, coupled design obligations across hardware and software, and finite simulation and verification capacity converge to limit design velocity. AI assistance delivers value only when targeted directly at the specific engineering work delaying the next supported decision.](images/ch02-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch02-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which fading technology gains, coupled design obligations, and finite checking capacity converge on the work limiting the next supported decision."}

The resulting pressures vary across design programs, shifting which bottlenecks delay progress. Simulation throughput may limit one study, while software development, missing physical collateral, or formal verification limits another. The chapter brings these observations together to explain how architects can identify the work delaying a decision and assess where learned methods or conventional automation could help. The purpose is to target assistance on the basis of the design problem, rather than infer its value from complexity alone.

## The Redistribution of Architectural Design Effort

The moonshot in @sec-moonshot asks whether a design system can make exploring thousands of hardware–software alternatives practical. That ambition begins with a concrete engineering tension. Suppose an architect considers expanding an on-chip Level-2 (L2) cache from 2\ MiB to 4\ MiB to alleviate memory bandwidth pressure. In an abstract simulator, doubling capacity looks like an easy win: miss rates plunge. But in silicon reality, that extra 2\ MiB is a physical sea of millions of static random-access memory (SRAM) bitcells that consumes die area, increases wire delays across long metal interconnects,[^fn-rc-delay-c02] and inflates static leakage current. In a passively cooled mobile device with a strict 3\ W thermal envelope, that leakage penalty directly subtracts from the thermal headroom available to run compute cores at full frequency. A lower miss rate in simulation answers only a fraction of the architectural question.

[^fn-rc-delay-c02]: **Interconnect scaling and wire delay**: While transistor switching delays decrease as gate lengths shrink, wire delay scales unfavorably. As interconnect cross-sectional dimensions narrow at advanced process nodes, wire resistance ($R$) rises sharply while parasitic capacitance ($C$) plateaus due to fringing fields between densely packed lines. Consequently, distributed $RC$ wire delay across long global lines increasingly dominates cycle times, making large contiguous structures (such as wide cache arrays or cross-chip buses) physically impractical to access within a single clock cycle.

Software adds another choice. Tiling the computation could reduce the working set enough to use a smaller memory, at the cost of additional transfers or control. Comparing these alternatives requires the matching software as well as models of the memory and its implementation. The architect is choosing which hardware–software combination to investigate and which observations could distinguish them.

Earlier design abstractions help make that work manageable. A register-transfer level (RTL) description lets engineers express a circuit without placing every gate themselves.[^fn-rtl-c02] Synthesis and implementation tools supply more detailed representations, while functional and timing checks test different requirements. The historical examples in @sec-moonshot established this relationship between an abstraction and its supporting tools. The pressure examined here is how much work remains when more interacting choices must pass through those tools.

[^fn-rtl-c02]: **RTL as an architectural contract**: Register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions specify exact cycle-by-cycle state transfers between synchronous registers. While RTL serves as the legal contract for logic synthesis, equivalence checking, and timing signoff, its rigid binding of pipeline stages and clock domains makes automated architectural exploration challenging: modifying a datapath's latency or decoupling an interface often requires restructuring the entire RTL description rather than tuning a high-level parameter.

A *design path* carries a question through candidate construction, tool execution, and comparison. For the cache example, that path might compare two capacities under one workload and inspect their latency and energy estimates. It becomes a *design loop* when the results update the design information and guide another permitted action. An unfavorable energy estimate might lead to a smaller capacity increment or a tiled software variant. Executing a fixed sweep supplies observations; using those observations to choose the next experiment closes the loop.

Each additional experiment consumes some combination of implementation effort, tool time, and review. Its inputs may span timing constraints, power intent, RTL configurations, and workload traces.[^fn-eda-constraints-c02] The limiting work might be preparing those inputs, constructing an alternative, or checking its consequences. Diagnosing that limit requires understanding why architecture choices have become more closely coupled. The changing contribution of device scaling provides the starting point.

[^fn-eda-constraints-c02]: **EDA constraint formats**: Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) describe timing requirements and power intent for electronic design automation (EDA) tools. Implementation and verification tools use those declarations to check the design under the specified conditions.

## Technology Scaling Breakdown and Specialization Pressures {#sec-fracturing-technology-dividend}

For roughly thirty years, processor performance advanced under classical Dennard scaling, where shrinking physical device dimensions reduced transistor area and gate delay while voltage scaling allowed more transistors to switch faster without increasing power density (@tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison) [@Moore1965Cramming; @DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Today, device technology still supplies transistor density, but it no longer delivers proportional gains in frequency, single-thread performance, or energy efficiency. Extracting performance now requires choices that tightly bind microarchitecture, software mapping, and physical implementation together.

### The Collapse of Dennard Scaling and the Shift to Specialization

To see why specialization became more attractive, consider the balance in the original scaling model. Classical Dennard scaling assumed that shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ reduced transistor area by $1/\kappa^2$, gate capacitance by $1/\kappa$, supply voltage by $1/\kappa$, and switching delay by $1/\kappa$. With switching activity held constant, $P_{\mathrm{dyn}} = \alpha C V_{dd}^{2} f$ then scaled by $(1/\kappa)(1/\kappa^2)(\kappa)=1/\kappa^2$ per transistor. This reduction exactly counteracted the $\kappa^2$ increase in transistor density and kept dynamic power density constant.

The post-Dennard column in @tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison uses one deliberately simplified assumption set to isolate what changes when voltage and frequency scaling stop: transistor area continues to shrink by $1/\kappa^2$, gate capacitance per transistor falls by $1/\kappa$, and transistor density rises by $\kappa^2$, while activity factor $\alpha$, supply voltage $V_{dd}$, and operating frequency $f$ remain fixed. The dynamic-power calculation excludes leakage and interconnect capacitance, which do not obey this ideal active-device model.

| Device Parameter | Classical Dennard Scaling ($\kappa > 1$) | Simplified Post-Dennard Case | Limiting Physical Constraint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transistor Area ($W \times L$)** | $1/\kappa^2$ | $1/\kappa^2$ | Gate pitch scaling continues |
| **Supply Voltage ($V_{dd}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Leakage and switching-speed trade-off |
| **Gate Capacitance ($C_{\text{gate}}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1/\kappa$ *(idealized)* | Gate and interconnect capacitance scale differently |
| **Operating Frequency ($f$)** | $\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Thermal dissipation and leakage limit frequency gains |
| **Dynamic Power Density ($P_{\mathrm{dyn}} / A$)** | $1$ *(constant)* | $\kappa$ *(under stated assumptions)* | Dark silicon and thermal limits |
: **Classical Dennard scaling versus a simplified post-Dennard case.** Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ historically kept dynamic power density constant while increasing operating frequency. With voltage, frequency, and activity held fixed in the displayed post-Dennard case, dynamic power density rises by $\kappa$; leakage, interconnect, and nonideal geometric scaling make real product behavior implementation-dependent. {#tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison tbl-colwidths="[24,24,28,24]"}

Writing transistor density as $\rho$, the post-Dennard dynamic-power-density ratio follows directly from that assumption set:
$$
\frac{P_{\mathrm{dyn}}'/A'}{P_{\mathrm{dyn}}/A}
= \frac{\alpha'}{\alpha}
  \times \frac{C'}{C}
  \times \left(\frac{V_{dd}'}{V_{dd}}\right)^2
  \times \frac{f'}{f}
  \times \frac{\rho'}{\rho}
= 1 \times \frac{1}{\kappa} \times 1^2 \times 1 \times \kappa^2
= \kappa.
$$
Dynamic power per active transistor therefore falls by $1/\kappa$, but the $\kappa^2$ increase in transistor density raises dynamic power per unit area by $\kappa$. In physical silicon, static subthreshold leakage, interconnect RC parasitics, nonideal density scaling, and dynamic power management govern the realized power density.

The classical balance broke down in the mid-2000s as supply voltage became harder to reduce. Lower voltage slows switching unless threshold voltage also falls, but lowering the threshold increases off-state leakage.[^fn-subthreshold-slope-c02] Device physics therefore constrains a trade-off that engineers must make among speed, active power, and leakage; it does not prescribe one operating voltage for every design. As voltage reductions slowed, architects could no longer count on density scaling alone to deliver the earlier combination of frequency and energy-efficiency gains [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach].

[^fn-subthreshold-slope-c02]: **Subthreshold slope and the thermodynamic leakage limit**: A field-effect transistor does not switch off instantaneously below its threshold voltage ($V_{\text{th}}$); instead, drain current decreases exponentially with gate voltage. The steepness of this turn-off is governed by the subthreshold swing $S = \ln(10) \cdot (k_B T / q) \cdot (1 + C_{\text{dep}} / C_{\text{ox}})$, which has a fundamental thermodynamic lower bound of approximately $60\ \text{mV/decade}$ at room temperature ($300\ \text{K}$). Reducing $V_{\text{th}}$ by $180\ \text{mV}$ increases off-state standby leakage current by three orders of magnitude ($10^3$), creating unmanageable static dissipation that prevents continuous voltage scaling.

Fifty years of microprocessor scaling data from Karl Rupp's CPU frontier (1971–2021), joined with a 2012–2024 frontier compiled from the published specifications of twenty-three accelerators including GPUs [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @JouppiEtAl2021TenLessons; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @AMD2025CDNA3; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2013K20XBoardSpec; @AMD2021CDNA2; @Myrhang2023AMDInstinctHPC; @Intel2023Gaudi2Datasheet; @Intel2024Gaudi3Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet; @Cerebras2019WSE; @Cerebras2021WSE2; @Cerebras2024WSE3], map this architectural evolution across three eras (@fig-microprocessor-trends). In the *device-scaling era* (1971–2005), single-thread performance, clock frequency, and transistor density all climbed by orders of magnitude, though at different rates. Around the 2005 Dennard boundary, clock frequency stalls near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$, and single-thread performance growth falls from about 52% per year (1986–2003) to about 23% per year, then to single digits by the late 2010s [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. This slowdown ushered in the *parallelism era* (2005–2016), where architects turned to multicore integration. Hardware thread counts reached 96 by 2016 and 128 by 2020, while peak CPU package power rose from about $200\ \text{W}$ in the mid-2010s to about $290\ \text{W}$ by 2021. A third inflection around 2016 marks the *specialization era*. CPU clock frequency and power flattened while CPU transistor counts kept rising, and the steepest scaling frontier migrated to domain-specific accelerators.

![**Frequency stalls while transistor budgets and accelerator power frontiers surge.** Karl Rupp's CPU frontier (1971–2021) joined with a 2012–2024 running-maximum frontier of accelerators, including GPUs, with published specifications. After 2005, clock frequency stalls near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$ and single-thread growth slows, while packaged accelerator transistor counts reach 208 billion (4 trillion in Cerebras wafer-scale parts) and accelerator thermal design power (TDP) reaches $1{,}000\ \text{W}$ [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Accelerator sources are cited in the text.](images/fig-microprocessor-trends){#fig-microprocessor-trends width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale line chart from 1971 to 2026 showing CPU and accelerator scaling across the device-scaling, parallelism, and specialization eras. CPU clock frequency flattens after 2005 and single-thread performance growth slows, while accelerator transistor counts and TDP rise steeply through 2024."}

These diverging curves in @fig-microprocessor-trends illustrate the structural end of automatic frequency scaling and the resulting pivot to specialized architectures [@Sutter2005FreeLunch]. When supply voltage scaling stalled around 2005, power constraints capped the fraction of transistors that could switch simultaneously at peak frequency, creating the *dark silicon* wall [@EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon].[^fn-dark-silicon-c02] In the parallelism era, duplicating cores extracted concurrency from parallel workloads, but serial bottlenecks and thermal limits bounded the return on general-purpose multicore expansion.

The specialization era visible after 2016 resolves that dilemma not by halting device scaling, but by reallocating silicon budgets to specialized datapaths. While CPU clock frequency remains capped near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$ and CPU power plateaus below $300\ \text{W}$, the accelerator frontier branches upward. Packaged accelerator transistor budgets climb from 15.3 billion in the NVIDIA Tesla P100 (2016) to 208 billion in the dual-die Blackwell B200 (2024), while Cerebras extends integration to 4 trillion transistors on a single wafer-scale die. Concurrently, accelerator TDP escalates from $300\ \text{W}$ to $1{,}000\ \text{W}$ per package. Specialization succeeds in this regime because regular matrix and tensor operations amortize instruction handling across massive arithmetic arrays, enabling continued throughput gains even though clock rates are no higher than they were twenty years earlier.

[^fn-dark-silicon-c02]: **Dark silicon**: Silicon that cannot all operate concurrently at full performance within the available power and thermal budget. Power gating, clock gating, and reduced operating rates are among the ways a design manages that limit.

### The Limits of In-Core Microarchitectural Scaling

General-purpose processors continue to improve through branch prediction, speculative execution, wider issue, and better memory hierarchies. These mechanisms can expose and exploit more instruction-level parallelism, but their benefits must pay for the structures needed to coordinate that work.

The issue window illustrates the difficulty. More entries let an out-of-order processor find ready instructions farther ahead, while greater issue width lets it execute more of them together. Yet completing instructions must broadcast their result tags to waiting entries, and selection logic must choose among the ready instructions. Enlarging the window increases the loads on those broadcasts; widening issue also increases comparisons and forwarding connections. The number of connections and the delay of the resulting circuit are different quantities, so a quadratic connection count is not itself a quadratic delay law. In particular, wakeup latency scales with content-addressable memory (CAM) tag broadcast lines across waiting entries, while selection latency is governed by arbiter priority trees across ready instructions. The implementation analysis of @PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective shows why wakeup, selection, and bypass structures can limit the benefit of wider machines.[^fn-palacharla-circuits-c02] Wire delay further constrains the physical distances over which that coordination can occur within a cycle [@AgarwalEtAl2000ClockRateVersusIPC].

[^fn-palacharla-circuits-c02]: **Issue-window circuit limits**: In an out-of-order superscalar core with issue window capacity $W$ and issue width $I$, the wakeup logic broadcasts $I$ result tags across all $W$ waiting instructions every cycle, requiring $I \times W$ content-addressable memory (CAM) comparators whose wire loading scales with window size. Ready instructions then feed selection logic, which uses priority arbiter trees whose gate delay grows with $\log W$ and whose layout routing introduces heavy wire capacitance. In deep-submicron processes, the physical wire delay across these densely routed CAM and arbiter structures, combined with the $O(I^2)$ forwarding paths of the bypass network, makes widening issue width beyond 8 to 10 instructions cycle-time prohibitive [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective].

Pipeline depth introduces a related trade-off. Dividing work across more stages can support a higher clock rate, but a branch misprediction may discard more work and take longer to recover from. Intel's 31-stage Prescott pipeline is a prominent example of this balance [@BoggsEtAl2004Pentium4NinetyNm]. Frequency alone cannot show whether the resulting processor completes a workload sooner or uses less energy. Moving to multiple cores changes the comparison again: coherence, memory ordering, synchronization, and workload partitioning determine how much parallel hardware is useful. These costs explain the appeal of specialization without implying that general-purpose microarchitecture has stopped advancing.

### The Specialization Turn and Accelerator Scaling

Specialization offers another use for the transistor budget. Regular computations can execute on many arithmetic units with less instruction-control overhead, provided that the workload exposes enough parallelism and the memory system supplies the operands.

Between the Pascal P100 and Hopper H100 generations, peak half-precision floating-point (FP16) arithmetic throughput outpaced off-chip memory bandwidth by roughly an order of magnitude (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier a). With precision held fixed and excluding structured sparsity,[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02] this divergence reflects an architectural pivot. P100 relies on conventional vector units, whereas subsequent generations integrate dedicated matrix Tensor Cores. The comparison illustrates the combined effect of specialized datapath acceleration and successive process nodes rather than an automatic application speedup [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper].

[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02]: **Structured vs. unstructured sparsity**: Mathematical weight pruning sets near-zero parameters to zero, but arbitrary (unstructured) sparse matrices introduce irregular memory indexing and load imbalance that frequently degrade performance on parallel vector and matrix hardware. In contrast, hardware-supported structured sparsity (such as NVIDIA's 2:4 pattern introduced in the Ampere architecture) enforces that exactly two out of every four contiguous values in a matrix must be zero. This fixed structural constraint allows dedicated multiplexing hardware to compress storage by $2\times$ and double dense matrix math throughput without the runtime overhead of sparse graph traversal.

Because arithmetic capacity expanded far faster than High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) supply, feeding these datapaths demands dramatically higher data reuse. Defining a workload's *operational intensity* as the arithmetic operations executed per byte transferred across the memory boundary, dividing peak compute rate by memory bandwidth yields the off-chip balance point (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier b). Across these four generations, that balance point escalates tenfold from 29 to 295 FLOP/byte. A kernel operating below that threshold cannot reach peak compute throughput even with zero control stalls, remaining fundamentally bandwidth-bound. A kernel operating above it provides enough reuse to clear the memory bottleneck, though it may still encounter pipeline dependencies, load imbalances, or tail latency.

![**Arithmetic scaling outpaces off-chip memory bandwidth.** (a) Growth relative to P100 in dense FP16 peak throughput, HBM bandwidth, and thermal design power (TDP) across four GPU generations (2016–2022). (b) The off-chip balance point escalates tenfold from 29 to 295 FLOP/byte, demanding steeper operational intensity to saturate peak arithmetic. Hardware specifications exclude structured sparsity [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper].](images/fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier){#fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel chart for P100, V100, A100, and H100 GPUs. First panel shows dense FP16 peak throughput growing much faster than HBM bandwidth and TDP relative to P100. Second panel shows the off-chip balance point rising tenfold from 29 to 295 floating-point operations per byte transferred from HBM."}

This steep divergence between arithmetic throughput and memory supply forces a decisive shift in how architects balance the machine. To prevent matrix engines from idling while waiting for operands, designers can respond by restructuring algorithms for temporal reuse, changing the computation to higher-density formats, widening physical interfaces with advanced packaging, or allocating substantial die area to on-chip SRAM caches.

These responses carry different costs. More SRAM can reduce off-chip traffic but consumes die area; wider memory interfaces and advanced packaging can supply more bandwidth but add implementation and power-delivery obligations. Software tiling can improve reuse within either organization. The useful choice depends on the workload's capacity, bandwidth, latency, and power needs. Memory is central to this comparison without being the limiting resource for every workload.

### Domain Specialization Tightens Cross-Layer Stack Coupling

Memory and thermal bottlenecks blur traditional stack boundaries. While the stack abstraction cleanly separates device physics, architecture, and software, domain specialization forces co-optimization across shared power and area budgets. Specialization does not create this coupling; instead, it tightens existing cross-layer dependencies.

Traditional layered abstractions isolate responsibilities between software optimization, microarchitecture, and device technology, but domain specialization binds these tiers across shared physical budgets (@fig-tao-vs-taos). While a layered view separates concerns for modular reasoning, the coupled reality dictates that a software tiling choice directly sets on-chip memory capacity, that memory capacity dictates die area and wire delays, and those physical limits in turn restrict which software schedules remain viable. Because these layers are physically coupled by power, thermal, and area constraints, an architectural change in one layer ripples through the entire stack.

![**Specialization makes cross-layer dependencies explicit.** (a) A classical layered view separates optimization, architecture, and technology into modular tiers. (b) The specialization-coupled view reveals how domain specialization binds software mapping, microarchitecture, and silicon fabrication across shared power, thermal, and area constraints.](images/fig-tao-vs-taos){#fig-tao-vs-taos width="80%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side stack diagrams. The first panel shows optimization, architecture, and technology stacked in a top-down hierarchy. The second panel introduces a specialization block coupled across all three tiers, bounded by a shared thermal, power, and area constraint perimeter."}

An early model must therefore retain the dependencies that can change the ordering of alternatives. A compute-only model may favor a larger arithmetic array even when its data supply makes the added units ineffective. Once that accelerator joins a larger system, communication and unaccelerated work introduce further reasons for a local improvement to disappoint. Those composition costs are the next part of the argument.

## Balancing Specialization and System Composition

When conventional technology scaling no longer yields automatic performance and energy gains, specialization becomes the primary architectural lever. Yet a specialized block is useful only as part of the system that supplies its work and consumes its results. Its local speedup must pay for dispatch, data transfer, and the work left on the host. Partitioning that system across chiplets or a wafer-scale fabric adds choices about where those costs occur. The first comparison is therefore what to accelerate and how much of the workload benefits.

### Specialization Traps and Amdahl's Law

Specialization spans a continuous spectrum rather than a binary leap from a general-purpose CPU to a custom accelerator. Designers can integrate vector and matrix units into general-purpose cores, assign data-parallel workloads to GPUs, construct domain-specific accelerators with custom dataflows, or restrict execution to specific operations in fixed-function application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Moving along this spectrum trades the breadth of workloads and software paths the hardware can execute for potential gains in energy efficiency and throughput density.

This spectrum redefines what architectural comparisons must weigh. While microarchitecture and multicore scaling refine a general-purpose foundation, specialization bends hardware around a specific workload. Evaluation metrics must therefore shift to reflect the expanded design space under study. Optimization targets differ fundamentally between an energy-constrained mobile system-on-chip (SoC) (optimizing milliwatts and joules per frame) and a warehouse-scale data center (optimizing total cost of ownership (TCO) and throughput per kilowatt). A specialized block can only be fairly judged against the specific target it was engineered for.

The potential upside is large. For the H.264 video encoder studied by @HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency, a fixed-function ASIC was roughly 500 times more energy efficient than the four-processor chip multiprocessor the authors started from. The authors captured most of this efficiency gain by eliminating instruction fetch, decoding, and redundant data movement, while simultaneously exploiting massive parallelism and fused operations. This result does not guarantee identical gains across the board. Instead, it highlights why deciding what to specialize, determining which flexibility to keep, and shaping the software interface have become central architectural challenges.

This drive for specialization has spawned a wide diversity of designs, a period the team behind Project Brainwave, Microsoft's deep-learning acceleration platform, described as one of rapid architectural diversification [@ChungEtAl2018Brainwave]. Publicly announced AI accelerators span seven orders of magnitude in peak power and six orders in peak performance across training and inference workloads (@fig-accelerator-landscape) [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS]. Ranging from subwatt embedded chips to multi-kilowatt data-center clusters, with energy-efficiency contours stretching from 100\ GOps/W to 100\ TOPS/W, these roughly 180 designs form a dense, heterogeneous cloud rather than clustering around a single operating point.

```{python}
#| label: fig-accelerator-landscape
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **AI accelerators span seven orders of magnitude in operating power.** Each point represents a
#|   publicly announced accelerator from the MIT Lincoln Laboratory survey, plotted as peak performance against
#|   peak power on log-log axes; the 180 parts span about $1\ \text{mW}$ to $23\ \text{kW}$ and
#|   $6\ \text{GOps/s}$ to $3.5 \times 10^7\ \text{GOps/s}$ [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS]. Marker shape and color denote form factor (circle chip, square card, triangle system), filled versus hollow markers
#|   distinguish training from inference parts, and dashed diagonals trace constant energy-efficiency contours
#|   from $100\ \text{GOps/W}\text{ to }100\ \text{TOPS/W}$. The resulting design space forms a dense, heterogeneous cloud
#|   rather than clustering around a single operating point.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-log scatter plot of about 180 AI accelerators, peak performance in giga-operations per second versus peak power in watts. Points span from subwatt embedded chips at the lower left to multi-kilowatt data-center systems at the upper right, roughly seven orders of magnitude in power and six in performance. Dashed diagonal lines mark constant energy efficiency from 100 giga-ops per watt to 100 tera-ops per watt. Chips are circles, cards squares, and systems triangles; training parts are filled and inference parts hollow."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
from _python.labels import place_labels

apply_style()

# Data: MIT Lincoln Laboratory AI accelerator survey, 2025 edition
# [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS], one row per publicly announced accelerator with a
# stated peak performance and power. Values are dataset-transcribed.
# Accessed 2026-07-19. Source data: data/datasets/chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
rows = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for d in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        try:
            perf = float(d["peak_performance_ops_per_s"]) / 1e9
            power = float(d["power_w"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        rows.append({"label": d["label"], "perf": perf, "power": power,
                     "form": d["form_factor"], "iort": d["inference_or_training"]})

forms = {"Chip": COLORS["workload"], "Card": COLORS["methods"], "System": COLORS["evidence"]}
markers = {"Chip": "o", "Card": "s", "System": "^"}  # shape as well as hue
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
xline = np.array([1e-3, 1e5])
for eff, lab in [(1e2, "100 GOPS/W"), (1e3, "1 TOPS/W"), (1e4, "10 TOPS/W"), (1e5, "100 TOPS/W")]:
    ax.plot(xline, eff * xline, ls=(0, (5, 4)), color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    x_pos = max(2.4e-3, 10.0 / eff)
    ax.text(x_pos, eff * x_pos * 1.3, lab, fontsize=4.6, color=COLORS["muted"],
            rotation=34, rotation_mode="anchor", va="bottom", ha="left", zorder=1)
for form, color in forms.items():
    for iort, filled in [("training", True), ("inference", False)]:
        pts = [d for d in rows if d["form"] == form and d["iort"] == iort]
        if not pts:
            continue
        xs = [d["power"] for d in pts]
        ys = [d["perf"] for d in pts]
        if filled:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolors="white", edgecolors=color, linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.95, zorder=3)
for txt, x, y in [("Very low power", 0.02, 3.0e3), ("Embedded / autonomous", 3.0, 1.2e1),
                  ("Data-center cards", 5e1, 2.5e6), ("Data-center systems", 1.5e4, 2.5e5)]:
    ax.text(x, y, txt, fontsize=5.2, fontstyle="italic", color=COLORS["muted"], ha="center", va="center", zorder=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(8e-4, 7e4)
ax.set_ylim(3, 1e8)
ax.set_xlabel("Peak power (W)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Peak performance (GOps/sec)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker=markers[f], ls="", markerfacecolor=c, markeredgecolor=c, markersize=5, label=f) for f, c in forms.items()]
handles += [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=COLORS["ink"], markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Training"),
            Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Inference")]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3, borderaxespad=0.4)
curated = ["Maxim", "GAP9", "Jetson1", "Perceive", "A100", "TPU4", "H100",
           "AMD-MI300X", "B200", "Gaudi3", "CS-2", "DGX-H100", "GroqNode", "Tachyum"]
by_label = {d["label"]: d for d in rows}
items = [(by_label[n]["power"], by_label[n]["perf"], n) for n in curated if n in by_label]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.095, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)
```

The spread in @fig-accelerator-landscape illustrates the range of deployment targets. It does not establish which design is best: the points mix numerical precisions, supported operations, and chip, card, and system boundaries. A subwatt sensor processor may emphasize local storage and low-precision computation to avoid costly transfers. A data-center accelerator may devote much more power to arithmetic and memory bandwidth. Within either setting, the architect still needs workload measurements to choose vector lengths, scratchpad sizes, dataflows, and scheduling policies. A favorable location in a peak-performance plot cannot replace that comparison.

Operating points in this design space also conceal fundamental differences in how operands reach arithmetic units. Commercial architectures diverge across streaming vector processors, systolic matrix arrays, reconfigurable spatial dataflows, and wafer-scale fabrics. Systolic arrays maximize local operand reuse through rigid register-to-register pipelines, while streaming multiprocessors rely on massive multithreading and deep cache hierarchies to tolerate memory latency. Wafer-scale designs eliminate board-level interconnect bottlenecks entirely by routing communication over unbroken silicon. Because each organization imposes distinct constraints on compiler scheduling, memory access patterns, and runtime invocation overhead, peak throughput and power ratings alone cannot determine which machine best serves a given workload.

In a composed system, a domain-specific accelerator (DSA) may handle dense compute while a general-purpose core retains control flow and irregular tasks. The runtime must move data and synchronize execution between them. Before committing die area and power to the specialized block, architects therefore need to determine what fraction $f$ of the workload it accelerates and how much the crossing costs. Amdahl's law makes that first comparison explicit (@eq-amdahl-communication).

$$S_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \frac{f}{S_{\mathrm{accel}}} + t_{\mathrm{comm}}}$${#eq-amdahl-communication}

where $S_{\mathrm{accel}}$ is the execution speedup on the specialized block, and $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is the added transfer and synchronization time, normalized to baseline execution time. The expression assumes that this added cost does not overlap useful computation. If targeted kernels consume half the total time ($f=0.5$), executing them ten times faster ($S_{\mathrm{accel}}=10$) with zero transfer overhead yields only `{python} f'{1 / (0.5 + 0.5 / 10):.1f}'` times total speedup [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. Adding communication lowers that benefit. The same reasoning bounded design-schedule improvements in @sec-moonshot; here it helps decide whether a proposed accelerator deserves its system cost.

The interpretation also depends on whether the problem size is fixed. Gustafson's law considers increasing the parallel work as more processors become available, as a training study might do with a larger model or dataset [@Gustafson1988AmdahlLaw]. A fixed-work latency comparison asks a different question. For an illustrative mobile-XR target of 120 frames per second (FPS), one frame interval is `{python} f'{1000 / 120:.2f}'` ms; this frame rate is a study assumption, not part of Lighthouse's initial requirements. If the per-frame work and deadline are fixed, dispatch and synchronization consume time that additional arithmetic cannot recover. The compiler, runtime, memory traffic, and residual host work must therefore accompany the accelerator in the comparison.

That judgment can be made quantitative. Amdahl's $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ lumps every communication cost into one normalized term, whereas the LogCA model separates the terms an offload actually pays: latency, overhead, granularity, computational index, and acceleration [@AltafWood2017LogCA]. For a payload of $g$ work units, host cost $C_h$ cycles per work unit, fixed invocation overhead $o$ in cycles,[^fn-host-dispatch-overhead-c02] local compute acceleration $A$, transferred data $d$ in bytes per work unit, link bandwidth $B$ in bytes per cycle, and overlapped transfer interval $T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)$ in cycles (or, equivalently, with time expressed in nanoseconds, work in FLOPs, and bandwidth in gigabytes per second):

[^fn-host-dispatch-overhead-c02]: **Mechanics of invocation overhead ($o$)**: In production systems, launching work on an off-chip accelerator typically involves assembling command buffers in host memory, pinning virtual memory pages, issuing a kernel-mode driver trap (`ioctl`), translating addresses via an input-output memory controller, and writing to a memory-mapped hardware doorbell register over Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe). This software traversal incurs hundreds of nanoseconds to several microseconds of latency ($o$). Modern accelerator interfaces reduce this penalty using user-space submission queues (such as Linux `io_uring` or direct hardware queue doorbells), but the fixed dispatch overhead remains prohibitive for fine-grained kernels.

$$
T_{\mathrm{host}}(g) = C_h g,
\qquad
T_{\mathrm{acc}}(g) = o + \frac{C_h g}{A} + \max\left(0,\frac{d g}{B} - T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)\right).
$$

The ratio of the two is the delivered speedup (@eq-logca-speedup-bound):

$$
S(g) = \frac{C_h g}{o + C_h g/A + \max\left(0,\, d g/B - T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)\right)}.
$${#eq-logca-speedup-bound}

In the nonoverlapped regime ($T_{\mathrm{overlap}} = 0$), offloading achieves net acceleration ($S(g) > 1$) only when the payload exceeds the break-even granularity $g^*$, obtained by setting $S(g) = 1$:

$$
C_h g = o + \frac{C_h g}{A} + \frac{d g}{B}
\implies
g\left[C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right) - \frac{d}{B}\right] = o
$$

which yields

$$
g^* = \frac{o}{C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right) - \frac{d}{B}}.
$${#eq-logca-breakeven-g}

For a positive invocation overhead and $A>1$, this break-even granularity exists only when the denominator is positive. If we take one work unit to be one arithmetic operation, then $d = 1/\mathrm{OI}$ in bytes per operation. This connects the transfer constraint to the operational-intensity reasoning of the Roofline model [@Williams2009Roofline]. When intensity falls to or below

$$
\mathrm{OI} \le \mathrm{OI}^* = \frac{1}{B \cdot C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right)}
$$

the denominator of @eq-logca-breakeven-g becomes nonpositive. At the specified acceleration $A$, transfer takes at least as much time per operation as offloading saves, so no payload size produces a speedup. Increasing $A$ changes the threshold, but cannot eliminate the transfer cost. This distinction separates an invocation cost that a larger payload can amortize from a per-operation cost that it cannot.

A break-even phase diagram maps the boundary where an offload transitions from a net performance penalty to a speedup (@fig-ch09-logca-phase-diagram). The horizontal floor of each curve reflects fixed host invocation overhead ($o$) relative to host cycle cost ($C_h$) and local acceleration factor ($A$). Lowering $o$ reduces the work needed to amortize each launch. The vertical asymptote, or operational intensity wall, is set by link bandwidth ($B$), where insufficient arithmetic reuse causes transfer delays to overwhelm computation savings. A larger payload can amortize fixed launch overhead, but it cannot overcome an operational intensity that falls to the left of the link bandwidth wall.

![**Launch overhead and link bandwidth set the minimum useful offload.** Modeled break-even granularity ($g^*$, where speedup $S(g)=1$) against operational intensity for seven interconnect regimes ($C_h=0.4\ \text{ns/FLOP}$, $A=50$, zero transfer overlap), using a nonoverlapped model adapted from LogCA [@AltafWood2017LogCA; @Williams2009Roofline]. Link bandwidths are nominal per-direction rates of each standard; invocation overheads $o$ are illustrative assumptions, not specified or measured values. Under these assumptions, the 15\ ns on-package case breaks even near 40\ FLOPs, while the 850\ ns to 4.5\ $\mu$s board and network cases need $10^3\text{--}10^4$\ FLOPs.](images/fig-ch09-logca-phase-diagram){#fig-ch09-logca-phase-diagram width="80%" fig-alt="Log-log line chart of modeled break-even offload granularity in FLOPs versus operational intensity in FLOPs per byte for seven interconnect regimes from Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) to InfiniBand. Each curve falls steeply near its bandwidth wall and then flattens at a floor set by its assumed invocation overhead, from about 40 FLOPs for the on-package case to about ten thousand for the cluster network."}

The plotted curves are illustrative model evaluations for named interconnect regimes, with host cost fixed at $0.4\ \text{ns/FLOP}$, local acceleration $A=50$, and no transfer overlap. They use per-direction link bandwidth and host invocation overhead, not bandwidth per millimeter of die edge or physical-link latency alone. For example, the advanced-package UCIe case uses one x64 module at 32\ GT/s ($B=256\ \text{GB/s}$) with an assumed $o=15\ \text{ns}$; the PCIe Gen 5 x16 case uses $64\ \text{GB/s}$ with an assumed $850\ \text{ns}$. The bandwidths follow from each standard's lane count and signaling rate; the overheads are chosen only to span on-package to cluster-network regimes. These assumptions let the reader compare the mechanisms while holding host and accelerator performance constant. They do not establish an offload threshold for every implementation of a standard, because driver, runtime, and protocol behavior also contribute to $o$.

Under the displayed assumptions, low startup cost and high link bandwidth permit smaller offloads. Higher-cost links require larger payloads, and nonoverlapped transfers reduce the asymptotic speedup even after startup has been amortized. The local factor $A$ is an upper bound in this model, approached only as the other costs become negligible. Estimating that gap requires a plausible invocation path, not just a datapath design.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{18\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The unamortized offload wall"}
**The trap.** In an illustrative scenario consistent with the model above, a mobile neural processing unit (NPU) adds a 1,024 multiply-accumulate (MAC) systolic tensor engine capable of $100\times$ local matrix-multiply acceleration ($A=100$) over unvectorized scalar RISC-V execution ($C_h = 1\ \text{cycle/operation}$), and the team treats that local factor as the expected system speedup.

**The mechanism.** Suppose the host executes scalar instructions at one cycle per operation ($C_h = 1$) and the runtime invokes the NPU through kernel-mode driver calls for each small layer (payload $g=500\ \text{operations}$). With launch latency $o=1{,}500\ \text{cycles}$, even an optimistic calculation omitting transfer costs gives $S(g)=500/(1{,}500+500/100)\approx0.33\times$. The offloaded path is slower than baseline scalar execution before direct memory access (DMA) transfer costs are included. Crucially, if the host processor is equipped with vector extensions (such as RISC-V Vector or AVX-512) processing multiple elements per cycle ($C_h \ll 1$), the denominator of @eq-logca-breakeven-g shrinks further, pushing the break-even granularity $g^*$ by another order of magnitude and severely widening the offload penalty.

**The lesson.** Local compute acceleration ($A$) cannot overcome unamortized startup ($o$) and transfer ($d g/B$) costs, especially when competing against an optimized, vectorized host core. Compiler layer fusion and kernel batching are required to increase payload size $g$ comfortably above the true break-even threshold.
:::

The interconnect and invocation path set the transfer and startup costs. The compiler and runtime help determine the payload size, data reuse, and overlap that the workload achieves. The offload bound also shows where the operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers reach their limits. A Layer 2 search that tunes array dimensions, buffer capacities, or unroll factors inside a frozen container can change $A$ and, through reuse, the transferred data $d$. It cannot change the invocation path that sets $o$ or the link that sets $B$, because those belong to interfaces the container holds fixed. For a workload whose operational intensity sits well below $\mathrm{OI}^*$ in @eq-logca-breakeven-g, such a sweep can at best move the threshold slightly, since $\mathrm{OI}^*$ approaches $1/(B \cdot C_h)$ however large $A$ becomes.

Moving the interface is a different kind of change. Kernel fusion, user-space submission queues, persistent kernels, and custom instruction extensions each alter $o$, $d$, or the payload $g$, and conventional hardware–software co-design teams make exactly these changes today. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) would be permitted to propose such interface changes alongside the hardware parameters, but whether it can do so better or more cheaply than a conventional team remains to be demonstrated. The offload bound will therefore return as a software question after we consider how the hardware is composed.

### Packaging and Chiplet Composition Risks

Specialized intellectual property (IP) blocks rarely ship in isolation. Teams integrate them into systems-on-chip (SoCs) or distribute functions across chiplets. Smaller dies can improve manufacturing yield under random-defect models, but packaging, assembly yield, test, and interconnect costs also matter [@Murphy1964CostSize; @FengMa2022ChipletActuary]. Reusing a chiplet across products can spread its development cost over more units, and different functions can use different process nodes. These benefits depend on compatible interfaces and a workable physical implementation. UCIe standardizes die-to-die communication, including physical interfaces and protocol support [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec], but does not choose the partition or establish that a particular package meets its power and shoreline-bandwidth needs.[^fn-shoreline-bandwidth-c02]

[^fn-shoreline-bandwidth-c02]: **Shoreline bandwidth density**: The communication bandwidth available per unit of die edge, often expressed per millimeter. In a side-by-side chiplet arrangement, interface placement, connection pitch, and signaling rate constrain the bandwidth that can cross the available edge.

Composition also introduces blocks whose implementation the system architect cannot inspect fully. Arm has supplied processor IP as fixed hard macros [@Arm2013CortexA15HardMacro], and Intel distributes encrypted RTL [@Intel2024EncryptedRTLIP]. Integration then relies on documented behavior, supplied models, and checks at the accessible interfaces. An interface specification such as Arm's Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) defines handshake and transaction-ordering rules at the boundary [@Arm2020AXI], but reset, clock-domain crossing, or coherence assumptions that fall outside that contract can still make two individually qualified blocks fail together. Shared network-on-chip (NoC) traffic adds another interaction: adequate average bandwidth can coexist with contention that misses a deadline. Partitioning must also provide test access, since finding a defective die before assembly avoids spending a package on it [@IEEE2020Std1838].[^fn-kgd-yield-c02]

[^fn-kgd-yield-c02]: **The known-good die (KGD) compound yield penalty**: In a multi-chiplet package comprising $N$ discrete dies, the overall package yield obeys a multiplicative compound law, $Y_{\text{package}} = Y_{\text{assembly}} \cdot \prod_{i=1}^N Y_{\text{die}, i}$. If eight chiplets with an untested wafer yield of 90% ($Y_{\text{die}} = 0.90$) are assembled into a single package with 98% assembly yield, final package yield drops to $0.98 \times (0.90)^8 \approx 42\%$, discarding nearly 60% of all finished products. The known-good die (KGD) methodology uses rigorous at-speed probe testing prior to dicing and bonding to guarantee that each bare chiplet is fully qualified, preventing defective silicon from consuming expensive advanced packaging interposers.

Automated exploration must account for those constraints. Missing rules waste evaluations on infeasible combinations; overly restrictive rules exclude viable ones. The Semiconductor Research Corporation's Microelectronics and Advanced Packaging Technologies (MAPT) roadmap identifies inconsistent supplier data formats, syntax, and semantics as obstacles to automation [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. A study should encode the constraints it knows and identify which remaining assumptions require integration tests or supplier clarification. Unknown compatibility should remain an unresolved condition, rather than silently become either permission or prohibition.

### Wafer-Scale Communication Trade-offs {#sec-wafer-scale-communication-tradeoffs}

Wafer-scale integration explores a different balance between local communication and physical scale. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE) distributes computation and SRAM across a single $46{,}225\ \text{mm}^2$ die, about the largest square a $300\ \text{mm}$ wafer can yield (@fig-cerebras-wse-scale). Keeping more computation and storage on the wafer can reduce transfers over board-level links, but power delivery, communication distance, and defect tolerance constrain how much of that hardware can be used [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS; @PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU].

![**Wafer-scale integration contrasts physical scale against reticle-limited dies.** The first-generation Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine ($46{,}225\text{ mm}^2$, 1.2 trillion transistors, 400,000 cores, and 18\ GB of on-chip SRAM) is about the largest square a $300\text{ mm}$ wafer can yield. The scale drawing sets it beside the $815\text{ mm}^2$ NVIDIA V100 GPU die, about 57 times smaller in area [@Cerebras2019WSE; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta]. Its cores communicate over interconnect that crosses reticle boundaries on the wafer. Keeping computation and communication on-wafer avoids board-level serdes bottlenecks but requires specialized solutions for power delivery, active heat dissipation, and hardware redundancy to bypass manufacturing defects.](images/fig-cerebras-wse-scale){#fig-cerebras-wse-scale width="70%" fig-alt="Scale drawing of a 300 millimeter wafer circle containing a 215 by 215 millimeter wafer-scale engine square, with an 815 square millimeter GPU die drawn to the same scale in one corner, about 57 times smaller in area."}

The WSE's internal SRAM bandwidth describes a different memory boundary from the HBM bandwidth in @fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier and should not be read as a directly interchangeable specification. Bringing more memory onto the wafer changes which transfers remain local; the benefit depends on how the workload maps onto the distributed storage and compute. In a wafer-scale GPU case study, physical constraints reduced usable capacity from a nominal 100 GPU modules to 40 [@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU]. The example shows why available silicon area is not equivalent to usable compute. Placement, routing around defects, and software scheduling determine the communication that the workload actually experiences. Across these packaging choices, the same question persists: can the software use the proposed organization well enough to justify its costs? Answering it requires an executable software path.

## Workload Volatility and Software–Hardware Coupling

The offload example makes software part of the architecture question. A compiler may fuse operations into a useful payload, while a runtime may add enough dispatch overhead to erase the benefit. The design must therefore include a way to program, schedule, and drive the hardware. That path also evolves: software can improve on fixed silicon, and new workloads can change which hardware features matter. These are two distinct challenges: making a proposed mechanism usable and understanding whether it will remain useful.

### Executable Software Paths

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The *executable software path* connects a programming model or front end to the compiler, libraries and kernels, runtime, driver or firmware, and relevant operating-system and deployment controls. Different systems need different combinations of these components. What matters is that the workload reaches the hardware with its intended behavior and without losing the expected benefit to overhead or data movement. A peak floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) specification does not establish that this path exists.

One way to organize that work is a *compiler narrow waist*: a shared intermediate representation (IR) through which multiple programming models and hardware targets pass. Common transformations can operate on the IR, while target-specific lowering maps operations onto a particular machine. Halide separates an algorithm from its execution schedule [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM]; Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) provides infrastructure for transformations across levels of abstraction [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR].[^fn-mlir-c02] Such abstractions can share work across targets, but each target still needs suitable lowering, runtime support, and validation.

[^fn-mlir-c02]: **MLIR dialect ecosystem**: Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) avoids a monolithic intermediate representation by organizing transformations into modular, domain-specific *dialects*. High-level tensor operations (such as linear algebra in the `linalg` dialect) undergo progressive lowering through structured control flow (`scf`) and arithmetic dialects down to low-level hardware representations (`llvm` or vendor-specific GPU dialects like `nvvm`), enabling optimizations to execute at the level of abstraction where domain semantics are most readily preserved.

Software development and porting effort accumulate rapidly across the compiler and runtime stack as specialized hardware primitives multiply (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall). In low-level template libraries such as CUTLASS, exposing new matrix instructions demands thousands of lines of architecture-specific templates and inline virtual assembly (PTX) statements (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall a) [@NVIDIACUTLASS]. Domain-specific compilers like Triton share a compiler core across targets, yet their target-specific backend code has grown faster than that shared core (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall b) [@TilletEtAl2019Triton], and production serving frameworks such as vLLM still accumulate native custom kernels to raise inference throughput (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall c) [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. Source-code counts document this expanding implementation footprint without directly measuring engineering maintenance hours.

![**Software support grows in both shared and target-specific components.** Source lines counted at selected release tags by a retained script. (a) CUTLASS architecture-specific headers grow from about 4,000 to about 208,000 lines, and inline `asm volatile` statements pass 3,000. (b) Triton's shared C++ compiler grows, while the NVIDIA and AMD backend trees that appear at v3.0 together outgrow it. (c) vLLM's native kernel sources grow from about 2,500 to about 120,000 lines; v0.27 reorganizes them, so its subdirectory split is not comparable [@NVIDIACUTLASS; @TilletEtAl2019Triton; @KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. Lines of code describe implementation footprint, not total maintenance cost.](images/fig-ch09-software-porting-wall){#fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall width="100%" fig-alt="Three-panel stacked bar chart of lines of source code at selected release tags. CUTLASS header code grows to about 690 thousand lines with an architecture-specific share that jumps after 2024, and inline assembly statements rise to about 3,000. Triton grows to about 280 thousand lines, with NVIDIA and AMD backend code appearing in 2024. vLLM native kernel code grows to about 120 thousand lines."}

For the architect, the important consequence is that a hardware feature can add software development and maintenance work. A new matrix instruction needs a mapping that uses its operand layout; an asynchronous transfer mechanism needs scheduling and synchronization that preserve correctness. A shared compiler can reduce duplication, while hand-tuned kernels may expose capabilities it does not yet support. Neither route removes the need to evaluate the resulting program.

An executable software path bridges high-level programmer intent and physical hardware execution by funneling representations through a compiler narrow waist (@fig-codegen-narrow-waist). Front-end abstract syntax trees (ASTs) lower into mid-level intermediate representations such as MLIR and LLVM IR, where target-independent loop transformations and memory optimizations occur. Lowering stages then map these operations onto target-specific machine instructions and accelerator dataflows under physical power and timing constraints. Crucially, the resulting binaries and runtime drivers close the evaluation loop by providing the concrete artifacts required to verify functional correctness, kernel performance, portability, and software maintenance overhead.

![**Executable target software paths connect developer intent to verification checks.** High-level domain-specific abstract syntax trees (Python, Triton domain-specific languages [DSLs]) lower through mid-level control-data flow graphs (CDFGs) in MLIR dialects and LLVM IR at the compiler narrow waist, where workload intent, architectural mechanisms such as CPU instruction set architecture (ISA) extensions and NPU dataflows, and silicon constraints converge. Lowered machine code and runtimes are subsequently evaluated against verification checks for correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability.](images/fig-codegen-narrow-waist){#fig-codegen-narrow-waist width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of an executable target software path showing programming models, compiler representations, libraries, runtimes, and generated code connecting hardware constraints to correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability checks."}

The break-even bound in @eq-logca-breakeven-g makes the stakes of that interface precise. In the nonoverlapped model, acceleration pays only when operation granularity $g$ exceeds $g^*$ and operational intensity stays above $\mathrm{OI}^*$. The compiler and runtime influence both. Fusing operations can create offload payloads large enough to amortize $o$; eliminating intermediate tensor allocations in off-chip memory can shrink the transferred data per work unit $d$. These choices move a kernel along the phase diagram in @fig-ch09-logca-phase-diagram.

Loop scheduling and instruction selection also determine how effectively a lowered kernel uses the target's register file and avoids pipeline stalls. In scalable vector architectures such as RISC-V Vector (RVV), compilers choose the active vector length and register grouping ($LMUL$, the register group multiplier) to trade loop control overhead against register pressure. Setting $LMUL=8$ amortizes instruction issue by operating on wide register groups, handling up to $\text{VLMAX} = LMUL \cdot \text{VLEN} / SEW$ elements per iteration (where $\text{VLEN}$ is the hardware vector register length in bits and $SEW$ is the selected element width in bits). However, grouping 32 physical vector registers into eight-register bundles leaves room for only four active vector operands. In a fused kernel with multiple live intermediate tensors, this high register pressure causes register spilling to memory, collapsing operational intensity. Smaller groupings such as $LMUL=1$ or $LMUL=2$ retain 32 or 16 independent operands, reducing memory spills at the expense of executing more loop iterations.

This trade-off exposes a tension that peak vector width cannot settle. A larger register group processes more elements per instruction, but can force extra memory traffic when too many values remain live. Evaluating such a choice requires executable code on the relevant hardware or model, with the intended numerics, memory ordering, and application binary interface (ABI) preserved. Autotuners such as AutoTVM search compiler schedules [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]; a joint hardware–software study also changes the machine those schedules target. Each proposed pair needs a comparable evaluation before its apparent advantage can guide a hardware decision.

An executable path makes the comparison possible, but does not keep it representative indefinitely. Compiler and runtime improvements can change the value of an existing mechanism, and a new workload can change which mechanisms are useful. Those changes may arrive while the hardware is still being designed.

### Changing Software and Fixed Hardware {#sec-software-changes-faster-than-silicon}

Software and workloads can change during hardware development. An architectural comparison may therefore need revisiting before silicon ships even when the RTL is unchanged. A design optimized for one model or compiler may encounter different shapes, schedules, or data types in deployment.

Several parts of the target can shift during this interval, including key-value (KV) cache management,[^fn-kv-cache-fragmentation-c02] compiler scheduling, and serving batch size. Numerical formats introduce a further choice: supporting 8-bit floating-point (FP8), 4-bit integer (INT4), or block-scale formats changes the arithmetic and data paths needed in hardware.[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02] Software may adopt a new format after the design has fixed which operations it implements directly.

[^fn-kv-cache-fragmentation-c02]: **KV cache scaling and memory fragmentation**: In autoregressive Transformer generation, attention keys and values for previously generated tokens are cached in memory to avoid redundant recomputation. Because sequence lengths grow dynamically by one token at each generation step, allocators that reserve contiguous buffers for a worst-case sequence length (such as 8,192 or 128,000 tokens) cause internal and external fragmentation. @KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention measured that such systems left only 20% to 38% of the memory reserved for KV cache holding actual token state, wasting 60% to 80% of that KV-cache allocation. Their vLLM system introduces paged allocation (PagedAttention) to assign non-contiguous physical blocks dynamically as tokens are generated.

[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02]: **Block-scale formats**: Low-precision number formats amortize shared exponent or scale metadata across a block of elements rather than storing independent metadata for every element [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling]. Committing to one in silicon fixes datapath choices even as formats and workloads continue to evolve, requiring careful judgment of whether the choice will remain useful over time.

Before fabrication, hardware and software teams can revise the design together, although late changes become increasingly expensive. After fabrication, software can still expose more of the hardware's capability or adapt it to different uses. It helps to separate an implementation improvement on the same task from a change in the task itself. A faster kernel may strengthen the case for the existing design; a different model shape or accuracy target may require a new comparison. Neither conclusion follows merely from a version number changing.

The primary challenge lies in determining whether a software change invalidates an architectural comparison or leaves it intact. Detecting that two traces or software versions differ does not answer this question. Architects must identify which specific differences could reverse design decisions and determine which measurements will test that possibility.

Specialization makes some assumptions about the workload more consequential. General-purpose execution can preserve flexibility, at a possible cost in performance or energy efficiency. The design question is which assumptions are stable enough to build into hardware and which changes its remaining flexibility can accommodate.

The assumptions worth monitoring include the kernel family, data types and precision, memory behavior, programming interface, deployment quality-of-service targets, and operating conditions (@fig-domain-specificity-shapes). They need not remain unchanged. The question is whether a change exceeds the flexibility or margin built into the design.

![**Specialization depends on assumptions about the target workload.** The six groups identify changes that may affect the value of a specialized design. A change calls for checking the affected assumptions; it need not invalidate the design or require repeating every evaluation.](images/fig-domain-specificity-shapes){#fig-domain-specificity-shapes width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram in which six source-to-target conditions surround the specialization scope: kernel family, data and precision, memory behavior, program interface, deployment and quality of service, and operating change. A separate bar states that changes in any condition can increase the verification burden."}

For example, a larger working set may cross a scratchpad-capacity threshold and introduce transfers that the original evaluation did not include. A change in batch size may reduce the work available per offload. Both can change the terms of the earlier break-even calculation. By contrast, a software change that preserves those terms and the required behavior may leave that particular comparison intact. This is why identifying the affected assumption is more useful than treating all software change as equally disruptive.

AI workloads provide a bounded example where model scale and computational demands shift visibly. While convolutional inference with fixed shapes tends to be regular, dynamic behavior frequently emerges in autoregressive Transformer deployments due to growing key-value caches [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention], variable sequence lengths, sparse mixture-of-experts routing,[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02] or distinct prefill and decode phases [@AgrawalEtAl2024SarathiServe]. Furthermore, the emergence of reasoning models that allocate adaptive test-time compute (such as chain-of-thought search, speculative rollouts, and iterative verification) shifts the execution bottleneck from predictable, dense matrix multiplication toward dynamic tree exploration, variable context depths, and acute memory-bandwidth pressure during token-by-token generation.[^fn-test-time-compute-c02] To illustrate this evolution, Epoch AI reported a four- to fivefold annual growth in training compute for notable models through May 2024 [@SevillaRoldan2024ComputeGrowth]; our own least-squares fit to a frozen July 2026 snapshot of the same database yields about 4.4-fold per year (@fig-training-compute-growth) [@EpochAI2025AIModels]. While scaling compute does not automatically constitute workload drift, empirical performance gathered for one model scale or training regime does not transfer to another without re-evaluating memory traffic and software assumptions.

[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02]: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing**: A sparsely gated model activates only a subset of its expert subnetworks for each input [@ShazeerEtAl2017MoE]. Because this input-dependent routing forces memory traffic to vary from token to token instead of following one fixed schedule, hardware must be designed to serve highly dynamic memory demands.

[^fn-test-time-compute-c02]: **Test-time compute and reasoning workloads**: Unlike standard single-pass autoregressive generation, reasoning-oriented models expand compute during inference by generating extensive internal chains of thought, backtracking, and verifying intermediate hypotheses. This execution profile shifts hardware balance from static FLOP-dominated systolic arrays toward high-bandwidth, latency-sensitive memory systems capable of managing volatile, rapidly expanding key-value (KV) cache structures.

```{python}
#| label: fig-training-compute-growth
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A fit to the displayed notable-model records yields about 4.4-fold annual growth in training compute.**
#|   Each point represents a notable AI model from the Epoch AI database [@EpochAI2025AIModels] plotted on a
#|   logarithmic scale ($10^{14}$ to $10^{27}$ FLOP) against publication date (2010–2026), with frontier models

Points rise from about ten to the fifteenth FLOP in 2010 to over ten to the twenty-sixth by 2025, frontier models tracing the upper edge. A fitted line marks roughly 4.4-fold growth per year. AlexNet, AlphaGo Zero, GPT-3, and GPT-4 are labeled along the rising frontier."

import csv
import datetime
import math
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _year(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-training-compute.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for row in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        yr = _year(row["publication_date"])
        try:
            flop = float(row["training_compute_flop"])
        except ValueError:
            flop = None
        if yr and flop and flop > 0 and 2010 <= yr <= 2026.6:
            pts.append({"yr": yr, "flop": flop, "name": row["model"], "frontier": row["frontier"] == "1"})

years = np.array([p["yr"] for p in pts])
logf = np.array([math.log10(p["flop"]) for p in pts])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(years, logf, 1)
growth = 10 ** slope

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.3))
other = [p for p in pts if not p["frontier"]]
front = [p for p in pts if p["frontier"]]
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in other], [p["flop"] for p in other], s=8, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=2, label="Notable models")
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in front], [p["flop"] for p in front], s=12, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["workload"], edgecolor=COLORS["workload_ink"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=3, label="Frontier models")
xline = np.array([2010, 2026.5])
ax.plot(xline, 10 ** (intercept + slope * xline), color=COLORS["constraints"], lw=1.5, zorder=4)
ax.text(2018.0, 10 ** (intercept + slope * 2018.8), f"×{growth:.1f} per year", fontsize=6.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], rotation=29, rotation_mode="anchor",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9))

by_name = {p["name"]: p for p in pts}
landmarks = {"AlexNet": ("AlexNet", 6, -12), "AlphaGo Zero": ("AlphaGo Zero", -8, 11),
             "GPT-3 175B (davinci)": ("GPT-3", -8, 11), "GPT-4 (Jun 2023)": ("GPT-4", 6, 10)}
for key, (label, dx, dy) in landmarks.items():
    p = by_name.get(key)
    if p:
        ax.annotate(label, (p["yr"], p["flop"]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy),
                    fontsize=5.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["muted"], lw=0.45))

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(2010, 2026.7)
ax.set_ylim(1e14, 3e27)
ax.set_xlabel("Publication date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Training compute (FLOP)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2010, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022, 2025])
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_spine].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.13, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

Relating software change to hardware development requires more than a model's publication date. Public product announcements provide one visible timeline (@fig-silicon-cadence). Measured between first announcements, the selected Apple SoCs arrive `{python} min(apple_gaps_mo)`–`{python} max(apple_gaps_mo)` months apart. The NVIDIA A100, H100, and B200 arrive `{python} min(nvidia_gaps_mo[:2])`–`{python} max(nvidia_gaps_mo[:2])` months apart, but NVIDIA first announced Rubin only `{python} nvidia_gaps_mo[2]` months after B200, roughly two years before it planned to ship. These markers locate products in time but do not reveal the internal design durations or the dates when their architecture decisions became fixed.
