The announcement intervals in @fig-silicon-cadence place successive products in time. Internal development overlaps, and an announcement does not reveal when a particular architecture choice became expensive to change. Exposure to workload change must therefore be assessed for the design decision itself, using its expected lifetime and remaining flexibility.

Benchmarks are how computer architecture holds changing workloads stable long enough to compare them, and they also show what that stability costs. Within one MLPerf version, division, scenario, and accuracy target, the run rules allow architects to compare results from different systems while leaving submitters free to optimize their own software [@ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. That comparability is maintained rather than inherent to the workloads, and it lasts only as long as the community continues maintaining the tasks and rules.[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02] When those rules change, an earlier comparison may no longer answer the same question.

[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02]: **Metrological traceability**: A measurement result is traceable when it can be related to a reference through a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing uncertainty [@NIST2021MetrologicalTraceability]. While architecture benchmarks do not create this kind of formal calibration chain, explicit versions for tasks, run rules, and measurement procedures remain essential so that reviewers can verify when two results remain genuinely comparable.

For a target such as mobile extended reality (XR), the application name is still too broad to specify an evaluation. Sensor processing, tracking, and neural rendering can have different deadlines and data-movement patterns. Lighthouse supplies a 3\ W target, but selecting an XRBench workload [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] still requires choices about traces, model versions, input distributions, and quality targets. Those choices complete a particular study; they should not be inferred from the name *XR*.

A useful comparison records these inputs and identifies changes that would require it to be repeated. Workload changes can also expose interactions beyond the original hardware boundary. If a faster kernel increases pressure on shared memory or communication, the architect may need to enlarge the study to understand the system benefit.

## Expansion of System Boundaries Across Compute Scales

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The system boundary determines which interactions an architectural comparison can reveal. Suppose one accelerator finishes a kernel sooner but sends more intermediate data over a shared network. A device-level comparison may favor it, while a service-level comparison finds that congestion delays the complete request. The relevant boundary has expanded because communication can change the ordering of the candidates. Architectural dependencies propagate across five compute scales, from individual execution cores to warehouse-scale data centers (@fig-architecture-levers). At each boundary, new system obligations alter candidate trade-offs: core-level hazards expand into accelerator offload latencies, chiplet shoreline bandwidth limits, wafer-scale defect bypasses, and data-center power distribution networks.

![**The study boundary must include interactions that can change the decision.** Five scales illustrate architectural dependencies from core execution to warehouse-scale deployment. A broader study may reuse component models; it need not reproduce every lower-level detail at the same fidelity.](images/fig-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of five architecture scales running from core through accelerator, system-on-chip or chiplet, wafer-scale system, and warehouse-scale system. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path, which carries constraints, interfaces, workload and software paths, tool feedback, failures, and rejected alternatives into one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

At warehouse scale, aggregate demand and availability requirements make resource placement and sharing architectural choices. The relevant system can include servers, networks, distributed software, shared cooling, and facility power limits [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Within and between nodes, interconnects such as Compute Express Link (CXL) introduce further choices about device and memory sharing.[^fn-cxl-c02] These mechanisms matter when they affect the objective under study, such as request latency, throughput, or cost of ownership.

[^fn-cxl-c02]: **Compute Express Link (CXL)**: A cache-coherent interconnect standard for processors, accelerators, and memory devices. Its memory semantics and switching support allow architects to treat device-attached or pooled memory as a system-level provisioning decision [@CXLConsortium2026CXL].

Evaluating all of those interactions at cycle-level detail is usually impractical. Architects combine component measurements with trace-driven or discrete-event models, controlled deployments, and production observations. The abstraction must preserve the behavior that matters: replaying independent requests may miss congestion, while mean service time may hide the slow responses that dominate *tail-at-scale* latency [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale]. Component failures and stragglers also need representation when they affect the comparison. Wider scope therefore changes the required models, rather than simply demanding a larger run of the same simulator.

A useful rule is to choose the smallest boundary that includes effects capable of changing the decision. For a local timing question, a block may suffice. For delivered service latency, shared resources may need to enter the model. Some choices can remain fixed while others are explored. Even with that discipline, the remaining hardware and software alternatives can multiply quickly, raising a separate question: how much of the resulting design space can the study afford to evaluate?

## Combinatorial Expansion of the Architecture Design Space {#sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search}

Once the study boundary is set, the architect must decide which alternatives to examine within it. Hardware parameters, software schedules, and compatibility constraints determine the candidate space. Its size matters, but only together with the cost of constructing and evaluating a candidate. A large space with cheap, useful feedback presents a different problem from a small space whose members each require days of implementation work.

Even when individual microarchitectural choices appear modest, their combinations multiply exponentially across the hardware-software stack. An illustrative system exploration evaluating five compute organizations, four instruction set architecture (ISA) and application binary interface (ABI) options, six memory hierarchies, four power targets, three compiler pipelines, and three process-library corners yields:

$$
5 \times 4 \times 6 \times 4 \times 3 \times 3 = 4{,}320 \text{ configurations}.
$$

Evaluating every candidate across three execution fidelities would require $12{,}960$ separate tool runs before filtering incompatible designs. A practical study rejects physically illegal combinations early, uses fast analytical estimates to screen the remainder, and reserves detailed cycle simulation and physical signoff for promising candidates. Candidate count alone does not dictate whether exploration is tractable; an analytical pass may score millions of points in seconds, while physical synthesis and static timing analysis limit throughput to a handful of candidates per day. A team must therefore price evaluation across stages before deciding whether its limiting bottleneck is producing candidates, screening them, or qualifying finalists.

The four tasks anchored in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors span the range that scale takes across hardware and software design. Candidate space volume does not measure evaluation work or decision confidence, because validity constraints and simulation fidelity differ radically between mapping, accelerator design-space exploration (DSE), floorplanning, and compiler tuning.

Timeloop [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop], an analytical framework for mapping and evaluating deep neural network (DNN) accelerators, illustrates a concrete lower bound on this combinatorial growth. For a convolutional neural network (CNN) layer with seven nested loops (batch size, input channels, output channels, output height, output width, kernel height, and kernel width) and a four-level memory hierarchy, loop ordering and level-bypass choices alone produce $(7!)^4 \times (2^4)^3$ arrangements. The first factor provides a different ordering of the seven loops at each of the four memory levels. The second factor yields a binary bypass choice at those four levels for each of three tensor data spaces (inputs, weights, and outputs). Factorization choices enlarge this mapspace even further. This formula represents neither the complete count nor a count of useful mappings; it isolates two sources of growth before legality, capacity, and performance constraints eliminate most candidates.

| **Architecture task** | **Scale anchor** | **Why candidate count is not enough** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DNN accelerator mapping | Timeloop enumerates loop permutations, factorization choices, and level-bypass alternatives [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. | Mapping is itself a combinatorial problem; architecture evaluation depends on the mapper and its constraints. |
| DNN accelerator DSE | MAESTRO, an analytical cost model for estimating DNN dataflow performance, reports 480M candidates, 2.5M valid designs, and 0.17M designs/s [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. | Pruning rules determine which candidates are evaluated and which are never seen. |
| Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) block floorplanning | AlphaChip uses reinforcement learning to generate macro placements [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. | Reported gains depend on the cases, baselines, compute budgets, and downstream checks, which remain disputed in the reproduction and reply [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. |
| Tensor-program tuning | AutoTVM, a machine learning-based tensor program optimizer, describes tensor-operator search spaces on the order of billions of possible implementations for a single GPU operator [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. | Compiler schedules create a hardware-dependent search problem of their own. |
: **Large search spaces place different demands on evaluation.** Mapping, accelerator DSE, floorplanning, and tensor-program tuning combine candidate scale, validity constraints, feedback cost, and different evidence requirements. {#tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

\FloatBarrier

Candidate scale emerges from entirely different parts of the system. While Timeloop and MAESTRO demonstrate how quickly mapping and accelerator choices multiply, AutoTVM illustrates that software scheduling creates a vast search space even after hardware parameters are locked. Floorplanning exposes the complementary limitation that rapidly generating a macro layout does not guarantee routability or timing closure. MAESTRO makes this distinction especially clear. Processing 0.17M designs per second enables evaluating its full 480M-candidate space in under an hour. In this scenario, analytical feedback is plentiful and fast; the challenging decision is determining which apparent winners justify more expensive evaluation.

The logarithmic scale in @fig-search-vs-eval-gap places this parameter sweep beside three published search-space estimates. The spread is useful for perspective, but the points represent different kinds of bounds: an illustrative architectural product, a reported accelerator exploration, an order-of-magnitude software estimate, and a mapping-space lower bound. They illustrate how scale manifests across different design layers rather than measuring the difficulty of a single task.

```{python}

#|   ($\sim 10^9$ implementations) [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM], and a Timeloop mapspace lower bound from loop-ordering

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(

    xticklabels=["$10^{2}$", "$10^{5}$", "$10^{8}$", "$10^{11}$", "$10^{14}$", "$10^{17}$"],

for y, row in enumerate(rows):
    ax.axhline(y, color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.65, zorder=0)
    if row["stated"]:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolor=COLORS["designspace"], edgecolor=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.2, zorder=3)
    ax.text(-0.86, y - 0.17, row["label"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.6, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(-0.86, y + 0.23, row["note"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["muted"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(1.04, y, row["right"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.1, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["designspace_ink"], clip_on=False)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

Together, these examples separate the size of a search space from the resources needed to learn from it. The next question is what more detailed evaluation reveals, and why a team cannot simply apply every available check to every candidate.

## Evaluation Bottlenecks Across Physical Feasibility, Simulation, and Verification

Evaluation becomes expensive for different reasons. A performance model may omit an implementation effect, a detailed simulator may run too slowly to cover a representative workload, and functional verification may require behaviors that ordinary workloads do not exercise. Distinguishing these difficulties helps determine which additional work would make a comparison more useful.

1. **Physical implementation:** Timing, routing, power delivery, and thermal behavior can change whether a candidate is feasible or attractive.
2. **Simulation throughput:** Detailed timing models, hardware emulators, and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) platforms require different investments in setup and execution.
3. **Functional verification:** Tests and proofs must address the relevant behaviors and properties, including interactions absent from performance workloads.

Any of these may limit a study. Physical constraints come first because they explain why a favorable high-level estimate may need revision before more evaluation is worthwhile.

### Physical Constraints {#sec-physical-constraints-move-into-architecture}

Physical effects create a tension between early comparison and implementation detail. A model simple enough to screen many candidates may omit a hotspot, supply-voltage drop, or routing constraint that changes the outcome. Detailed checks can expose these effects, but need more complete inputs and more tool time. The architect must decide which physical information is needed early and which uncertainties can wait until the candidate is developed further.

Power delivery and heat removal illustrate the problem on different time scales. When many units become active together, the changing current can cause a transient supply drop through the resistance and inductance of the delivery network.[^fn-di-dt-drop-c02] Whether that drop causes a timing failure depends on the operating point and available margin. Sustained activity creates a different question: can the package remove heat from the locations where it is generated? In a stacked design, the placement of active logic and the heat-removal path matter as well as total power. An average-power estimate alone answers neither question.

[^fn-di-dt-drop-c02]: **Inductive voltage transients ($L \frac{di}{dt}$)**: Power delivery networks contain parasitic inductance ($L$) distributed across printed circuit board planes, package balls, and micro-bumps. When an un-gated vector or matrix unit abruptly transitions from idle to full execution within one or two clock cycles, the rate of current change ($\frac{di}{dt}$) can exceed hundreds of amperes per nanosecond. The resulting induced voltage drop ($\Delta V = L \frac{di}{dt}$) compounds the steady-state resistive drop ($IR$), causing a transient voltage sag that can collapse the core supply rail below minimum operating voltage ($V_{\text{min}}$) and induce timing errors unless mitigated by on-die decoupling capacitors and conservative voltage guardbands.

The scaling discussion in @sec-fracturing-technology-dividend explains why a new process cannot be assumed to resolve these interactions. Logic cells, SRAM macros, and interconnects have different scaling behavior and implementation constraints. Returning to the opening cache example, the useful estimate is the area, access time, energy, and leakage of the available memory macro, together with its connections. A nominal process label does not establish those costs.

Data movement provides a useful quantitative example. The 45\ nm reference values collected by @Horowitz2014Energy place a 32-bit integer addition near 0.1\ pJ, SRAM accesses in the displayed range at 10–100\ pJ, and off-chip DRAM accesses at 1.3–2.6\ nJ (@fig-data-movement-energy-scale). The access widths and memory sizes differ, as labeled in the figure. These historical values illustrate why a small reduction in arithmetic can be outweighed by additional memory traffic; they are not energy estimates for a current process. A system estimate must combine the relevant operation counts with costs for its own implementation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-movement-energy-scale
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Data movement can dominate arithmetic energy.** Reference $45\ \text{nm}$ energy values from @Horowitz2014Energy
#|   demonstrate a disparity of more than four orders of magnitude between local arithmetic (0.1\ pJ for a 32-bit integer add)
#|   and memory access (10–100\ pJ for on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM), 1.3–2.6\ nJ for off-chip DRAM, a $13{,}000\text{--}26{,}000\times$
#|   energy penalty). Architectural comparisons must represent data locality, buffer hierarchies, and memory
#|   traffic rather than counting arithmetic operations in isolation. Transcribed order-of-magnitude anchors,
#|   not current-node device estimates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale plot comparing arithmetic and memory-access energy, showing a 32-bit integer add at 0.1 picojoules, static random-access memory (SRAM) accesses from 10 to 100 picojoules, and an off-chip DRAM access range from 1.3 to 2.6 nanojoules."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style, draw_range_rows, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Source dataset: data/datasets/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, 45 nm).
# Values are read from the CSV; ratios to the 32-bit integer add are computed here.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    src = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))]

baseline = float(src[0]["energy_low_pj"])


def _fmt_ratio(value):
    ratio = value / baseline
    return f"{ratio / 1000:.0f}k" if ratio >= 1000 and value >= 1000 else f"{ratio:.0f}"


rows = []
for r in src:
    low, high = float(r["energy_low_pj"]), float(r["energy_high_pj"])
    op, width = r["operation_or_access"], r["width_or_capacity"]
    if "SRAM" in op:
        capacity = width.replace(" 64 bit", "")
        label, note = f"{capacity} SRAM access", "64b access"
        color = COLORS["orange"] if high >= 100 else COLORS["green"]
    elif "DRAM" in op:
        label, note, color = "off-chip DRAM access", "64b access", COLORS["red"]
    else:
        label, note, color = f"{width.replace(' bit', 'b')} {op}", "local arithmetic", COLORS["blue"]
    right = f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}$\\times$" if low == high else f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}–{_fmt_ratio(high)}$\\times$"
    rows.append({"display_label": label, "display_note": note, "energy_low_pj": low,
                 "energy_high_pj": high, "right_label": right, "color": color})

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 3.2))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.40, right=0.80, top=0.82, bottom=0.08)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(0.06, 4000),
    xticks=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
    xticklabels=["0.1 pJ", "1 pJ", "10 pJ", "100 pJ", "1 nJ"],
    xlabel="rough energy per operation or access",
)
draw_range_rows(ax, rows, low_key="energy_low_pj", high_key="energy_high_pj", label_x=-0.82, right_x=1.04, label_fontsize=6.6, note_fontsize=5.4, right_fontsize=6.1, label_dy=-0.17, note_dy=0.23)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

To compare designs, we can group their energy costs by where the work occurs. The decomposition below separates computation, memory, interconnect, control, and leakage. Each term must be estimated for the workload and implementation being studied; the historical reference ratios do not supply those totals.
$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} = E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} + E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
$${#eq-system-energy-decomposition}

The decomposition in @eq-system-energy-decomposition gives the memory hierarchy an explicit place in the comparison. The *memory wall* described by @WulfMcKee1995HittingMemoryWall concerns the growing importance of memory stalls as processors improve faster than memory latency. Its consequence depends on how often the workload reaches the slower level and how much latency can be hidden. The energy comparison similarly depends on traffic, rather than access cost alone.

Communication among cores and accelerator tiles adds another term. Offered traffic can exceed a network-on-chip link's capacity, causing queueing and backpressure even when the arithmetic units have spare capacity. The physical layout must also provide the wires needed by the chosen topology. Network traffic congestion and physical routing congestion are related implementation concerns, but they are not the same phenomenon.

The proxy-mismatch failure appears directly when comparing total system energy between a balanced baseline design and an unoptimized accelerator candidate (@fig-waterbed-effect). The candidate shrinks compute energy ($E_{\mathrm{compute}}$), yet its added memory accesses and communication overhead swell memory and interconnect energy ($E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}}$) enough to push the system total above the baseline. Reducing compute energy in isolation can thus increase data movement and interconnect energy, inflating total system energy and causing partial evaluation metrics to rank an inferior design first.

![**Local compute energy reductions can obscure total system energy increases.** A stacked energy breakdown compares a balanced baseline against an illustrative accelerator candidate. While the candidate reduces compute energy ($E_{\mathrm{compute}}$), unoptimized data movement and interconnect traffic swell memory and interconnect energy ($E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}}$), pushing total system energy ($E_{\mathrm{system}}$) above the baseline and causing partial proxy metrics to rank the inferior design first. Bar heights illustrate structural trade-offs and do not represent measured circuit traces.](images/fig-waterbed-effect){#fig-waterbed-effect width="80%" fig-alt="Bar chart comparing a baseline energy breakdown with an illustrative candidate whose lower compute energy is outweighed by higher memory and interconnect energy."}

When evaluation omits data movement and wire parasitics, the missing energy terms are large enough to invert candidate rankings (@fig-waterbed-effect). While early analytical models can incorporate rough interconnect estimates, placement and routing ultimately dictate physical wire lengths, congestion, and parasitic capacitance [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. An automated search guided by an incomplete proxy score repeatedly exploits these omissions, systematically promoting brittle configurations that fail physical implementation. Comparing selected candidates with a more detailed model helps reveal that bias.

The same approach applies to power. Early activity and placement estimates can identify a dense mapping that deserves closer analysis even when average power is acceptable. Learned estimates such as PowerNet's IR-drop prediction [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet] can help screen appropriate designs; their validity depends on the inputs and conditions they cover. Electrical supply analysis and thermal analysis must then address their respective effects. A thermal result cannot establish that a rapid current transient is harmless.

Vector execution illustrates this policy interaction concretely. Adding 512-bit vector units to general-purpose CPU cores raises peak floating-point throughput. However, sustained wide-vector execution can raise switching capacitance and dynamic power enough to trigger processor downclocking (such as AVX-512 frequency licensing offsets), reducing the base clock for scalar operations on the same core. Peak vector width alone does not determine final application speed; architects must measure active-frequency policies alongside the exact mix of vector and nonvector work on the target processor.

During timing signoff, engineering teams evaluate multiple analysis views that pair operating modes with specific process corners using static timing signoff tools such as Cadence Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus].[^fn-pvt-corners-c02] A design can clear one view while failing another. Because physical-design tools rely on heuristic optimization, a single failed closure attempt rarely indicates whether the candidate or a flawed tool setup caused the failure. Comparing constraints, seeds, and repeated outcomes separates true design flaws from tool artifacts.[^fn-eda-tool-noise-c02]

[^fn-pvt-corners-c02]: **Multi-mode multi-corner (MMMC) timing closure**: Physical signoff tools must verify that a circuit functions reliably across wide operational extremes of process, voltage, and temperature (PVT). Critical paths are evaluated against competing extremes: "slow" corners (such as slow-slow transistor fab variation, lowest operating voltage, and maximum operating temperature) test for setup-time violations, while "fast" corners (fast-fast silicon, maximum supply voltage, and sub-zero temperatures) test for hold-time violations where signals race ahead of clock edges. At 3\ nm-class gate-all-around nanosheet nodes, signoff must also account for device self-heating and statistical on-chip variation, and the first nodes with a backside power delivery network (BSPDN), such as Intel 18A and TSMC A16, add its effects as well. A candidate design that simulates comfortably within cycle limits at nominal conditions may fail tapeout signoff due to hold violations or local electromigration under extreme PVT and thermal corners.

[^fn-eda-tool-noise-c02]: **EDA tool non-determinism and noise floors**: Physical synthesis, placement, and detailed routing rely on stochastic heuristics, including simulated annealing, force-directed relaxation, and multi-threaded maze routing. Minor variations in netlist declaration order or random seed initialization can shift worst negative slack (WNS) and total wirelength on identical RTL. The size of that spread depends on the tool, design, and flow, so it must be measured for the flow in use rather than assumed. In automated AI exploration loops, agents can easily mistake an artifact of tool noise for an architectural breakthrough, or discard a superior microarchitecture because the placer hit an unfavorable local minimum. Bounded multi-seed calibration is necessary to separate true architectural merit from tool noise.

Design-rule checks (DRCs) introduce further physical constraints. Routing must satisfy restricted design rules, including minimum wire and via spacing [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. Moving a single macro can spawn numerous violations, and repairing one can alter neighboring routes and expose fresh errors. If an automated flow cannot interpret these markers, it shifts a repetitive cleanup and rerouting burden onto implementation engineers.

An illustrative scenario shows where a Layer 2 optimizer can run into this friction. Suppose it sweeps macro floorplan coordinates $\theta$ inside a fixed die outline and scores each candidate with a fast wirelength estimate or learned surrogate. Such proxies can track average wirelength while missing local pin density, routing channel blockages, and multi-corner timing. If the favored placements crowd memory interfaces into dense clusters, the router may run short of tracks and return timing violations and design-rule markers that the proxy never predicted. Within the container, the optimizer cannot reshape pipeline registers, re-partition blocks, or change interface contracts, so the repair falls to implementation engineers unless the proxy is recalibrated or the search is allowed to move those boundaries. How often this happens depends on the design, the proxy, and the flow; the scenario identifies a failure to check for, not a measured rate.

Interpreting a later physical failure requires the exact design and assumptions that produced it. The retained RTL, parameters, constraints, and implementation outputs let an architect distinguish a design problem from a mismatched input. Electronic design automation (EDA) tools also consume representations beyond RTL, including Library Exchange Format / Design Exchange Format (LEF/DEF) and Liberty timing files.[^fn-lef-def-c02] The execution mechanics are developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces; here the consequence is that preparing and preserving compatible inputs is part of evaluation work.

[^fn-lef-def-c02]: **LEF/DEF and Liberty**: In place-and-route flows, LEF carries the abstract physical information used to place and connect blocks, while DEF records design-specific physical information, such as placement and routing, even before those steps are complete [@Si2LEFDEF]. Meanwhile, Liberty provides characterized cell models covering timing, power, noise, and related behaviors [@Synopsys2012LibertyFormat]. Physical design relies on these implementation formats to expose details omitted from high-level architectural descriptions.

Multi-fidelity methods pair inexpensive models with selected evaluations that resolve their important omissions [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. The appropriate check depends on the question: gate-level functional simulation, static timing analysis, and thermal analysis provide different information. Using a more expensive tool helps only if it addresses the uncertainty that could change the decision.

While an inexpensive energy proxy supports early screening, candidate finalists require an accurate power model before binding power or efficiency decisions can be made. A design can lead on advertised peak throughput yet degrade on real application workloads due to memory stalls and runtime overhead. One generation of AMD processors illustrates how wide that gap between an advertised specification and delivered work can open in practice.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** In the Bulldozer generation (Zambezi, 2011), AMD grouped two integer cores behind a shared front end and floating-point unit while pushing clock frequency hard [@BurgessEtAl2011Bulldozer]. Core counts and frequencies are easy to advertise, so they made compelling marketing points. In sharing those structures, the design team traded per-thread capacity for aggregate throughput.
**The gap.** Those figures did not reflect how real workloads used the machine. The shared structures became bottlenecks when threads competed for them, and the higher frequencies raised power draw. The later FX-9590 part carried a 220\ W thermal design power [@AMDFXQuickReference].
**The lesson.** Shared structures must be evaluated with workloads that expose contention, alongside power and frequency behavior. Core count and clock rate alone cannot settle that comparison. AMD's later Zen design placed renewed emphasis on per-core performance and efficiency [@AMDZen].
:::

Because physical constraints and reliability concerns define a vast search space, no early model eliminates the need for physical signoff tools to validate final claims. Architects must understand which lower-cost estimates are safe for broad screening, and which rigorous checks retain the power to overturn candidate rankings.

### Simulation Throughput and Fidelity {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

Once a model includes the effects needed for a comparison, execution time becomes a constraint of its own. Longer workloads and more candidate configurations compete for compute, tool licenses, and the time needed to interpret results. The question is how much representative behavior the available evaluation budget can cover.

At a representative detailed simulator throughput of ten to one hundred thousand target instructions per host second, simulating one second of a workload that retires one billion instructions in that interval takes $10^9/10^5$ to $10^9/10^4$ host seconds, or approximately `{python} f'{1e9 / 1e5 / 3600:.1f}'` to `{python} f'{1e9 / 1e4 / 3600:.1f}'` hours. Multiplying candidates or workload windows can therefore consume the budget quickly even when preparing each run is easy.

Architectural simulators, compiled RTL simulation, hardware emulators, and FPGA platforms offer different ways to trade setup effort against execution capacity. They also model different things. A fast architectural simulator may simplify timing interactions; Verilator executes an RTL model; FireSim uses FPGA acceleration to run full-system, cycle-exact RTL simulations [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Their accuracy must be judged for the behavior each model represents. An RTL model can represent functional details absent from an architectural model while still omitting routed wire delays or thermal behavior. The useful tool is the one whose model and execution capacity answer the study's question at an acceptable total cost.

Sampling can reduce execution cost without simply removing model detail. SimPoint selects representative program regions [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], while SMARTS uses statistical sampling with error estimates [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Analytical screening, sampled detailed simulation, and full-workload execution can therefore complement one another. A study should state which behavior the sample represents, how initialization and warmup are handled, and which conclusions require additional runs.

The allocation decision has two risks: a cheap estimate may discard a promising candidate or send an unsuitable one into an expensive evaluation. More representative simulation can reduce uncertainty about performance, but it does not establish correctness for every behavior the design permits. That remaining obligation leads to verification.

### Verification Bottlenecks

Verification faces an exponential state-space upper bound, even though careful structuring, abstraction, and advanced verification methods govern practical workload size. Adding a single state-holding flip-flop doubles the number of encoded states, meaning a design with $n$ sequential state elements can technically encode up to $2^n$ states. In practice, the reachable subset is far smaller because it depends on reset sequences and valid transition logic; verification flows therefore avoid blind enumeration of every encoded state.

For a large design, brute-force enumeration is generally impractical. Verification teams instead combine functional coverage targets, SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), formal checks, constrained-random and directed tests, regressions, and unresolved-defect reviews. Coverage describes the behaviors or requirements that the verification plan intended to exercise; a completed coverage target is not proof that every possible bug is absent. A new architectural organization can require new tests and properties even when much of the implementation is reused.

For these reasons, architectural evaluations must explicitly weigh verification effort alongside the classic pillars of power, performance, and area (PPA). For instance, a highly speculative cache-coherence protocol might demonstrate an impressive simulated throughput gain, yet it remains an unacceptable candidate if checking its labyrinth of transient states and race conditions exceeds the design-program budget.

Simulation and formal methods provide different kinds of assurance. Simulation exercises selected behaviors under supplied stimuli. A completed formal proof establishes a stated property for all behaviors covered by the model and its assumptions, but the solver may not be able to complete that proof. Bounded model checking (BMC) searches behaviors up to a specified depth; finding no counterexample within that bound is generally not an unbounded proof. Combinational equivalence checking asks whether two combinational descriptions compute the same Boolean function. These techniques can complement one another, provided that their scopes and assumptions remain explicit [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

The semiconductor industry has grappled with this verification pressure for over a quarter of a century. As far back as 2001, the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) Design chapter declared verification "a bottleneck that has now reached crisis proportions" [@ITRS2001Design]. Today, the Semiconductor Research Corporation's MAPT roadmap explicitly warns of a widening verification gap looming across future technology transitions [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. While this history makes verification an indispensable constraint to check whenever someone proposes generating architectural candidates faster, it does not imply that verification will be the limiting constraint in every design program.

Staffing surveys give one view of the work involved. In the 2022 Wilson Research Group study, demand for verification engineers on IC and ASIC projects grew at about 6.2% per year from 2007 to 2022, against about 2.7% per year for design engineers [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Compounded over fifteen years, that is roughly two and a half times the 2007 verification staffing against one and a half times the design staffing (@fig-verification-demand-scissors). These are relative changes in surveyed staffing, not measurements of the time needed to verify an additional candidate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Verification staffing grew faster than design staffing.** Mean peak staffing per IC/ASIC project
#|   indexed to a 2007 baseline demonstrates that verification engineer demand grew by 146% (a 6.2%
#|   compound annual growth rate [CAGR], reaching $\approx 2.46\times$) from 2007 to 2022, while design engineer demand grew by 50%
#|   (a 2.7% CAGR, reaching $\approx 1.50\times$) [@Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Filled markers indicate
#|   printed data labels from published survey figures; hollow 2022 markers represent chart-read approximations
#|   constrained by the study's stated growth rates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-line chart indexing engineer demand to 2007, with verification-engineer demand rising to about 2.5 times its 2007 level by 2022 while design-engineer demand reaches about 1.5 times, opening a widening gap between the lines."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Mean peak engineers per IC/ASIC project, Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA
# functional-verification studies (Foster's published summaries).
# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv. Rows with
# evidence_type == chart_read_constrained are drawn hollow; growth labels are computed.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    staff = [r for r in csv.DictReader(fh) if r["year"].isdigit()]
years = [int(r["year"]) for r in staff]
design = [float(r["design_engineers_mean_peak"]) for r in staff]
verif = [float(r["verification_engineers_mean_peak"]) for r in staff]
printed = [r["evidence_type"] == "printed_data_label" for r in staff]

design_idx = [v / design[0] for v in design]
verif_idx = [v / verif[0] for v in verif]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.80, top=0.93, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(years, verif_idx, color=COLORS["green"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.plot(years, design_idx, color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
for x, v, d, solid in zip(years, verif_idx, design_idx, printed):
    if solid:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=22, color=COLORS["green"], zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=20, marker="s", color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=26, facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["green"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=24, marker="s", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["blue"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)

ax.text(years[-1] + 0.6, verif_idx[-1], f"verification\nengineers (+{(verif_idx[-1] - 1) * 100:.0f}%)",
        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["green"], clip_on=False)
ax.text(years[-1] + 0.6, design_idx[-1], f"design\nengineers (+{(design_idx[-1] - 1) * 100:.0f}%)",
        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["blue"], clip_on=False)

ax.set_xlim(years[0] - 1, years[-1] + 1)
ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.7)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_yticks([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1.0$\\times$", "1.5$\\times$", "2.0$\\times$", "2.5$\\times$"])
ax.set_ylabel(f"mean peak demand vs. {years[0]}", fontsize=7)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The indexed lines in @fig-verification-demand-scissors show why verification capacity deserves explicit attention in a design plan. They do not identify the cause of the growth or determine the bottleneck in a particular project. The next comparison asks a different question: what do the surveys report about first-silicon outcomes alongside that effort?

Longitudinal industry survey data place these results in perspective (@fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors). In the Wilson Research Group studies, the published mean share of project time spent in verification stayed between 53% and 57% from 2010 to 2020, while the share of projects reaching first-silicon success fell from about 32% in 2020 to 24% in 2022 and 14% in 2024 [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. Because the survey populations and design complexities shift between study years, these trends do not establish that added verification caused worse outcomes. They do show that large verification investments coexist with persistent silicon respins, which the studies attribute most often to logic or functional flaws.

![**Verification effort stays high while first-silicon success falls.** Wilson Research Group values from Foster's published reports: the mean share of project time in verification (2010 to 2020), first-silicon success (2014 to 2024), and the verification-to-design staffing ratio (2007 to 2024; hollow points derived from the studies' stated growth rates). First-silicon success falls to 14% in 2024 [@Foster2013WilsonPart5; @Foster2015TrendsFunctionalVerification; @Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2021WilsonPart12; @Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy; @Foster2023WilsonPart12; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. Years without a published value are left blank, and population-level trends do not isolate causality within individual projects.](images/fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors){#fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors width="90%" fig-alt="Line chart of survey results from 2007 to 2024. The mean share of project time in verification stays between 53 and 57 percent from 2010 to 2020. First-silicon success falls from about 32 percent in 2020 to 14 percent in 2024. The verification-to-design staffing ratio on the right axis rises from 0.62 in 2007 to about 1.16 in 2024."}

The reported respin causes span logic, analog integration, clock-domain crossings, timing, and hardware–firmware behavior [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. Clock-domain crossings, for example, require attention to metastability as well as the logical sequence seen by a testbench.[^fn-metastability-c02] More random stimulus alone may poorly exercise a rare interaction; directed tests, suitable constraints, assertions, and formal analysis can target what is missing. The useful question is which failure mechanisms the current checks can detect.

[^fn-metastability-c02]: **Metastability and clock-domain crossings (CDCs)**: A bistable storage element enters a metastable state, remaining balanced between logic 0 and 1 for an unbounded settling time, when asynchronous inputs violate setup or hold timing constraints. In multi-clock systems-on-chip (SoCs), signals crossing asynchronous clock domains must pass through multi-stage synchronizers to reduce the probability of failure, because standard cycle-accurate testbenches cannot model intermediate analog voltage states.

Escaped defects also differ in how they can be repaired. Some permit a firmware or software workaround; others require revised silicon, and a workaround may sacrifice performance or functionality. Intel's \$475M charge associated with the Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) defect illustrates the potential cost of a shipped hardware error [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge]. Spectre and Meltdown illustrate a different problem, in which microarchitectural behavior undermines software's security assumptions [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. These cases motivate early detection without establishing one universal cost multiplier for every late defect.

A new candidate may need new verification work before its performance matters. Published RTL-generation benchmarks include failures at parsing, interface compliance, and functional testing [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. Those tests do not establish timing closure or system correctness, but they show why a plausible description is only a starting point. The cost and latency of producing and checking a candidate depend on its scope, the reused verification infrastructure, and the required assurance; there is no fixed generation-to-verification ratio across abstraction levels.

The same data bound what Layer 1 point assistance can be expected to deliver on its own. A generator that drafts an isolated leaf module or testbench inside a human-specified pipeline speeds up one part of implementation. The surveys place much of the effort elsewhere: verification staffing grew at more than twice the annual rate of design staffing (@fig-verification-demand-scissors), and verification occupied more than half of reported project time in the 2010 to 2020 studies (@fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors). The cost estimate discussed in @sec-design-cost-pressure points the same way, assigning most of a leading-node budget to software, verification, and IP qualification. Faster drafting therefore helps only if the drafted modules do not add more integration and checking work than they save, such as reconnecting mismatched ports, resolving clock-domain crossings, clearing lint violations, and debugging corner-case deadlocks. Whether they do is a measurement a team can make, not a conclusion to assume in either direction.

Crucially, attempting to resolve this bottleneck by using generative models to synthesize both RTL implementations and their verification testbenches creates an insidious *co-generation trap*. When an AI generator produces both the circuit under test and the assertion suite or test harness from the same specification prompt, both artifacts inherit the same generative priors and semantic blindspots. A subtle misunderstanding of an edge-case bus protocol or arithmetic overflow condition will be faithfully mirrored in both the hardware logic and the checking harness, resulting in passing test runs that mask catastrophic functional escapes. Rigorous automated verification therefore demands an independent, immutable verification oracle (such as formal SystemVerilog assertions derived from architectural contracts, golden reference transaction models, or mutated test suites) that the generative agent is prohibited from modifying.

Verification effort belongs in the architectural comparison when alternatives differ in the tests, properties, and integration work they require. Reusing a familiar interface may preserve much of that investment; changing the organization may require new checks. The resulting engineering cost, together with implementation and software work, determines which promising designs a program can afford to develop.

\FloatBarrier

## The Economics of Specialized Silicon {#sec-design-cost-pressure}

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The implementation and verification work described above consumes a finite development budget. Much of that work is non-recurring engineering (NRE): an investment in the design, software, and qualification that precedes production. Its scale matters both when choosing an architecture and when deciding how many alternatives to develop in detail.

Public estimates illustrate the size of this investment (@fig-design-cost-by-node). The most widely quoted series come from International Business Strategies (IBS). A 2018 IBS series put IC design cost at \$51.3M for a 28\ nm planar device, \$297.8M at 7\ nm, and \$542.2M at 5\ nm [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm], and the Semiconductor Industry Association quotes the same order of magnitude, more than \$540M for a 5\ nm design in 2020 [@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign]. Arm's 2023 prospectus, citing a July 2022 IBS estimate, gives \$249M at 7\ nm and \$725M at 2\ nm [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The two vintages disagree at 7\ nm, which is a reminder that each estimate rests on its own assumptions about die size, IP reuse, and what counts as design cost. Project budgets vary widely around any of these figures, but every published series shows development cost rising steeply toward the leading edge.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-by-node
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Leading-node design-cost estimates rise steeply, and they depend on the estimate's vintage.** Each bar is an
#|   International Business Strategies (IBS) estimate, labeled with the year of the IBS series it comes from
#|   [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm; @ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The two vintages differ at 7\ nm (\$298M versus \$249M),
#|   so the bars are published estimates under different assumptions, not a controlled node-scaling series or universal project prices.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of IC design-cost estimates by process node. The 2018 estimates are 51 million dollars at 28 nanometers, 298 million at 7 nanometers, and 542 million at 5 nanometers. The 2022 estimates, drawn hatched, are 249 million at 7 nanometers and 725 million at 2 nanometers."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv (rows with plotted == yes).
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")) if r["plotted"] == "yes"]
# Largest node first; within a node, older vintage first.
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (-float(r["node_nm"]), r["estimate_vintage"]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
positions = list(range(len(rows)))
for pos, r in zip(positions, rows):
    cost = float(r["cost_musd"])
    newer = r["estimate_vintage"].endswith("2022")
    ax.barh(pos, cost, height=0.58, color=COLORS["constraints_tint"], edgecolor=COLORS["constraints"],
            linewidth=1.4, hatch="////" if newer else None, zorder=3)
    ax.text(cost + 12, pos, f"${cost:,.0f}M", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7,
            fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], zorder=4)
    ax.text(cost + 100, pos, r["estimate_vintage"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6,
            color=COLORS["muted"], zorder=4)

ax.set_yticks(positions)
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{float(r['node_nm']):g} nm" for r in rows], fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 1000)
ax.set_xlabel("Estimated IC design cost (US$M)", fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
ax.grid(True, axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The composition of a design budget helps identify where assistance could matter. In the IBS 2\ nm estimate cited by Arm, software development, verification, and IP qualification together account for 71% of the total [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. This is a cost allocation for that estimate, not the fraction of every project's critical path. It nevertheless shows why faster RTL drafting alone cannot be assumed to remove most development expense.

The same allocation suggests a hypothesis about where each operational layer could reduce cost, which only measurements of real programs can test. The prospectus does not itemize the remaining 29%, so that share cannot be read as the cost of RTL drafting or physical design alone. Point assistance (Layer 1) that drafts leaf RTL acts on part of that remainder, so its effect on total NRE depends on whether the drafted code adds more review, integration, and verification work than it saves. Parameter search inside a qualified container (Layer 2) can preserve existing interface verification and qualified IP, which limits its verification cost but also limits the design changes it can reach. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) would target the 71% share only if it could generate verification collateral, compiler support, and qualification evidence that reviewers accept at lower total cost than conventional practice; no published program has yet shown that it can.

Production volume determines how that upfront investment contributes to each shipped unit. A simple accounting model makes the relationship explicit:

$$
C_{\mathrm{unit}} = C_{\mathrm{variable}} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{NRE}}}{V},
$$

where $C_{\mathrm{variable}}$ is the average manufacturing, packaging, and test cost per shipped unit, $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ is the allocated development investment, and $V$ is shipment volume. In silicon economics, $C_{\mathrm{variable}}$ is heavily governed by die area ($A$) and defect-density yield ($Y$): larger dies encounter lower wafer yields ($Y \approx e^{-A D_0}$ or negative binomial equivalents), multiplying the effective silicon cost per good die. This defect-limited area scaling is the primary economic justification for chiplet disaggregation: splitting an $800\ \text{mm}^2$ monolithic design into smaller modular dies dramatically recovers wafer yield, amortizing packaging interconnect overhead while preserving unit economics. The model omits financing, pricing, and time-to-market effects, but exposes the central trade-off. A specialized design may save enough energy or system cost to justify its development. At lower volume, those benefits must carry a larger share of NRE per unit. Specialization does not necessarily imply a small market, and a chiplet reused across products can increase the volume over which its development cost is spread.

For a mobile-XR program, the architectural question is whether the expected efficiency and functionality justify the custom hardware, software, and checking work at its anticipated volume. Reusing IP, retaining programmable execution for changing workloads, or choosing a less aggressive process may improve that balance. Each choice can also affect power, performance, and schedule. The useful comparison includes those consequences rather than assuming either that custom silicon is unaffordable or that specialization always pays.

An evaluation budget is part of the same calculation. Spending more on a simulation or integration test can be worthwhile if it resolves an uncertainty that would otherwise cause expensive redesign. Generating more candidates can also be worthwhile if they offer meaningful alternatives. Their value depends on what the complete study learns for the resources it consumes, which brings the chapter's separate pressures back together.

## Compounding Loop Pressures {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

The preceding sections examined distinct costs, but a design study encounters them together. A different memory organization may need new compiler support; that software changes traffic, which affects the physical and system comparison. Some candidates can reuse existing checks, while others require new verification work. The effort needed to learn from one alternative therefore depends on more than the cost of proposing it.

This tight coupling matters because optimizing one stage often shifts the bottleneck elsewhere. Generating candidates faster risks flooding the evaluation queue. Speeding up simulation risks churning out more results than reviewers can reconcile. Building a more accurate physical model may reveal that none of the available choices hit the target. Design-space size, evaluation capacity, and decision quality are distinct quantities; increasing the first does not guarantee improvement in the other two.

Rather than hunting for a single universal bottleneck, engineering teams should identify the specific work that throttles progress. Teams can measure the age and size of simulation or verification queues, track the fraction of candidates rejected as illegal, or count repeated tool runs and changing inputs. Reviewers can also monitor where results stall waiting for expert judgment. While broad industry trends provide context, local, concrete measurements are necessary to diagnose the actual constraints of a specific design program.

The MAESTRO anchor in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors helps make that diagnosis concrete. Its reported analytical throughput makes a large space affordable to score, so a program using such a model should examine work on either side of the search before paying for a faster optimizer. Upstream, a ranking depends on the workload description: changed layer shapes or batch sizes could make an otherwise accurate analytical comparison irrelevant to the deployment. Downstream, a recommendation about implementation may require checks the analytical tier cannot supply. These are possible bottlenecks for a program using the model, not findings that the cited MAESTRO study had stale workloads or an unvetted queue.

This diagnosis includes wasted work as well as slow work. A simulator run against the wrong workload occupies a slot without resolving the pending question, even if it completes successfully. Correcting the inputs can improve useful throughput without making the simulator itself faster.

This possibility extends the classic *design productivity gap*, documented in the 1999 ITRS and restated in its 2001 edition [@ITRS2001Design], and reiterated in the Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) and Semiconductor Industry Association Decadal Plan [@SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. Earlier abstraction shifts made larger designs tractable through RTL synthesis and IP reuse. Where candidate construction becomes cheaper, the corresponding challenge is whether simulation, verification, and review can absorb the additional work.

Not every constraint appears as a queue. A study may be waiting for a missing trace or supplier constraint, or its available organizations may all fail the target. In the latter case, faster evaluation of the same alternatives will not produce a feasible design. The architect may need to reconsider the organization, or the requirements, before scheduling more runs.

When the rate of candidate generation outpaces the throughput of physical evaluation and expert review, unvetted proposals accumulate in a widening *scissors gap* (@fig-scissors-gap). Beyond the crossover point where generation velocity exceeds downstream checking capacity, adding more generative throughput merely swells the backlog of unresolved proposals. This backlog is not an inevitable penalty of automated generation; admitting fewer candidates, filtering through hierarchical screening tiers, or scaling verification throughput can rebalance the loop.

The operational layers can push on either blade. Layer 1 point assistance mainly lowers the cost of drafting candidates, which widens the gap unless review and verification capacity grow with it. Layer 2 optimization automates selection within a container against fast surrogates, which removes some human triage but can move the accumulation to the physical checks when candidates fail on routing congestion, dynamic IR drop, or timing closure. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) is intended to couple exploration to stronger checks such as static timing analysis, design-rule checking, formal equivalence, and clock-domain crossing analysis, so that fewer unvetted proposals reach human review. Whether it narrows the gap depends on how much checking capacity it consumes and how often its surviving proposals still fail later review; that is a claim to measure, not a property the layer confers.

![**Unchecked candidate generation outpaces physical evaluation and review capacity.** Conceptual schematic illustrating candidate generation velocity outpacing physical evaluation and expert review throughput as architectural scope expands. Beyond the crossover point, unverified proposals accumulate into a widening *scissors gap* of unresolved candidates that have been generated but never evaluated rigorously enough to accept or reject. Accelerating proposal generation without scaling evaluation capacity expands this unvetted backlog.](images/fig-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="80%" fig-alt="Conceptual scissors diagram in which tool and reviewer capacity initially exceeds candidate volume before crossing at a central fulcrum. Diverging upper and lower blades open beyond the crossover, where candidate generation accelerates faster than physical evaluation capacity, opening a widening scissors gap of unsettled work."}

The diagram becomes a diagnosis only when a program's own measurements show this imbalance. Cheaper generation can encourage the team to admit more work, but the response is a choice about how to spend the saved effort. A familiar observation from resource economics helps explain why total demand need not fall when one activity becomes cheaper.

::: {.callout-law title="The Jevons Paradox of Automated Generation"}
**The principle.** Greater efficiency lowers the marginal cost of generation, encouraging increased consumption that can outstrip initial savings. Jevons first documented this rebound effect for coal consumption [@Jevons1865CoalQuestion]. In automated chip design, cheaper proposal generation increases total resource consumption if downstream simulation, verification, and engineering review capacity remain fixed.

**The design implication.** If cheaper RTL generation leads a team to submit more candidates to simulation and implementation checks, demand for compute and EDA licenses can rise. The generation saving remains real; the complete study may nevertheless consume more resources.

**The response.** Choose how many candidates to admit and which evaluations each needs, then measure total effort and useful results. Admission limits and staged screening are possible controls (@sec-law-jevons-paradox in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

## Targeting AI Assistance {#sec-where-ai-assistance-targets-design-pressures}

The diagnosis becomes useful when it changes where the team spends its assistance budget. If a missing executable artifact prevents evaluation from starting, drafting that artifact may advance the study. If hundreds of candidates already await simulation, another generator may add delay, while screening or tool automation may help. The same method can therefore be useful in one program and poorly targeted in another.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Relieve the True Limiting Constraint"}
**The principle.** Target optimization directly at the bottleneck that actively delays the design decision. Common limiting factors include stale architectural models, long physical simulation runtimes, unpruned candidate sets, and senior engineering triage overhead during failure interpretation.

**The application.** Assess whether assistance reduces the total effort or delay needed to answer the question. Include preparation and review costs, and preserve the checks that the decision requires. The limiting work may change as the study progresses.
:::

These needs suggest several possible uses of AI, from retrieving design information and screening candidates to drafting testbenches and guiding search. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization develops the method choices. Here the purpose is to connect a possible intervention to the work it could save.

For changing software, an automated regression pipeline can rerun the same benchmark with a new compiler and flag a change in candidate rankings. Assistance might help explain which transformation caused the change or identify an input mismatch. The comparison still needs to distinguish an implementation improvement from a changed task. Some of this work may be served well by conventional automation, without a learned model.

The rows in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound pair possible assistance with the engineering work it might reduce and the checks that remain. Keeping these together prevents a faster local task from being mistaken for a completed architectural comparison.

| **Limiting work** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What still establishes the result** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Context is scattered or stale | Reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information; flag missing details or stale assumptions. | Manual search across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and architectural judgment that the information is sufficient. |
| Strong evaluation is scarce | Estimate performance, power, physical risk, or uncertainty before a stronger tool is run. | High-fidelity evaluations spent on candidates unlikely to change design decisions. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design region, and checks on finalists. |
| A needed artifact is missing | Draft RTL, compiler code, tests, constraints, or candidate organizations. | Repetitive artifact creation and the initial pass through a design choice. | Interface rules, compilation or synthesis, verification, and physical checks appropriate to the artifact. |
| The choice space exceeds the budget | Search mappings, schedules, parameters, or topologies under stated objectives and constraints. | Manual sweeps and repeated selection among large numbers of choices. | A complete objective, legal choices, matched evaluation budgets, and stronger evaluation of the selected result. |
| Tool operation or triage consumes attention | Configure tools, launch runs, classify failures, compare reports, and route uncertain cases. | Repeated tool operation and initial result triage. | Clean tool state, reproducible commands, declared tool results, and expert review where required. |
: **Match assistance to the limiting work and retain the necessary checks.** Each row identifies a possible saving and the evidence needed to use its output in a design decision. {#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[22,28,24,26]"}

These roles do not determine the workflow by themselves. The operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers organize them by how much of the design the automated work may change. Applied to the limits in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound, point assistance (Layer 1) fits rows where one artifact is missing and the surrounding design is settled; its result still passes through the integration and verification work described above. Search inside a fixed container (Layer 2) fits rows where the choice space exceeds the budget but the interfaces are right, and it stops being useful when the limiting effect sits in an interface it cannot move, as with the offload overhead $o$ or a congested memory interface. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) would be the candidate response when the existing formulation itself excludes the useful organizations, with its exploration held to static timing, design-rule, formal, and power-integrity checks rather than to proxies. Prediction, generation, and optimization can contribute to all three; the distinction is how the design work is organized and which choices it can revisit.

The cost of assistance also belongs in the comparison. A surrogate may require data from expensive evaluations; generated candidates require checking; and tool-using systems consume compute, licenses, and review time. These investments may be worthwhile, but their omission can turn displaced work into an apparent saving.

Evaluation standards must also support rejecting AI assistance entirely. An established deterministic method that already solves the limiting task within budget is a serious alternative. A learned method has a poor case when representative training data are unavailable, an adequate independent check cannot be constructed, or training, inference, tool calls, and added review cost more than the engineering work saved. For the illustrative 4,320-candidate sweep, suppose the analytical tier can score every candidate within budget but cycle simulation and synthesis cannot. Under that assumption, a surrogate trained only to replace the cheap analytical calls may save little; a screening predictor calibrated against the expensive tiers is worth costing instead. The candidate count alone does not establish either conclusion. If the primary obstacle is an infeasible requirement, the appropriate response may be to reformulate the architecture question or decline further search.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{28\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="No single method carries the Lighthouse moonshot"}
**Context.** Lighthouse begins with an XRBench-class mobile workload, a 64-bit RISC-V basis, a 3\ W target, and a 3\ nm-class process. It leaves workload instances, memory organization, compiler support, and implementation choices to be developed into a study. The earlier cache and offload examples show why those choices must be considered together across the operational layers.

**Application.** A Layer 1 approach might ask a generator to draft an isolated vector arithmetic leaf cell or scratchpad controller, leaving engineers to connect buses, resolve clock-domain crossings, and debug races. A Layer 2 approach might fix the 64-bit pipeline and sweep cache capacities and unroll factors against a cycle simulator; it would stall if off-chip memory traffic pushed the design past the 3\ W envelope or dense macro placement congested routing, because neither fix lies inside the container.

A Layer 3 AI-native design system, if one could be built for this problem, would be permitted to set the processor template aside. From the XRBench intent and formal signoff assertions, it could propose a streaming tensor datapath, custom arithmetic, tiled scratchpad memories, and matched compiler loop schedules, and it would have to test them against the thermal limit with static timing and dynamic IR-drop analysis rather than proxies. No such system has yet carried this prompt through to a checked result.

**Outcome.** Deploying an AI-native design system requires proving both that the candidate satisfies all verified silicon constraints and that the workflow reduces total engineering cost. Merely chaining a generator to an EDA tool or outputting a novel design description does not establish an architectural advantage.
:::

The resulting test is practical: did the chosen assistance help the team answer its architecture question, with the required checks and an honest account of the work? A useful local tool can pass that test without carrying the complete Lighthouse workflow. A broader design system must demonstrate the additional capability its coordination is intended to provide. The architect remains responsible for interpreting the comparison and deciding what further work or review the result warrants.

\FloatBarrier

## Open Questions

The chapter explains why useful architectural progress can be limited by software, implementation, evaluation, or verification work. It does not establish which limit dominates a particular program, or how much an AI-native workflow can change that balance. The remaining questions concern those limits and the evidence needed to understand them.

- **Where does AI assistance produce sustained gains in real design programs?** The limiting work can move as a project develops, and a saving in one stage can add effort elsewhere. Measurements of complete studies are needed to distinguish shorter turnaround, better designs, and work merely shifted into preparation or review. How consistently can the initial diagnosis predict which intervention will help?

- **How should evaluation budgets adapt when search introduces a new organization?** A predictor or analytical model may be well characterized for the existing design family while saying much less about a generated alternative. Spending too little on the unfamiliar candidate can reject a useful idea; spending too much can exhaust the study. How should a design system allocate evaluations when model reliability changes along with the designs being explored?

- **How does architectural generation change the verification work?** Reusing known interfaces may preserve existing tests and properties, while redesign can create interactions that those checks do not cover. It remains unclear when automated generation reduces total engineering effort and when the required verification grows faster than the implementation saving. Can a design system recognize that difference early enough to guide what it proposes?

- **How much flexibility should hardware retain for software that does not yet exist?** Current workloads reveal the benefit of specialization, but cannot fully establish its lifetime value. Programmability, spare capacity, and alternative data paths provide different forms of adaptability at a present cost in area or energy. How can architects compare those investments when future workload changes are only partly known?

- **How can automated exploration use incomplete descriptions of third-party blocks?** Interface documents, supplied models, and observed behavior may each expose only part of a block's constraints. An exploration system must distinguish tested compatibility from assumptions that remain unresolved. What combination of supplier information and targeted testing is sufficient to compare new compositions without treating missing information as permission?

## Summary

Architectural gains increasingly depend on how microarchitecture, specialization, software, and physical implementation work together. The examples in this chapter make the consequences concrete: a faster arithmetic block can lose to offload overhead, a wider vector grouping can increase spills, and lower compute energy can be outweighed by memory traffic. A useful comparison includes the interactions capable of changing its outcome.

Investigating those alternatives consumes implementation effort, evaluation capacity, and verification work. A large search space does not by itself establish an expensive study, and an expensive study does not by itself establish a need for AI. The opportunity depends on the work that limits progress, the alternatives assistance could make practical, and the total cost of obtaining results that answer the architecture question. An AI-native design system is one possible response when the existing formulation excludes useful organizations; its value remains something to demonstrate.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Follow the costs of a local improvement.** Include data movement, control, software overhead, and physical effects before treating a block-level gain as a system gain.
- **Evaluate hardware with its software.** Compiler mappings, runtime behavior, and workload changes can alter which organization is useful.
- **Choose the boundary that answers the question.** Model the interactions that can change the decision, using appropriate abstractions for each scale.
- **Budget for learning from candidates.** Candidate counts, simulation throughput, verification effort, and development cost describe different constraints. Tests, models, and proofs also establish different things.
- **Target assistance and measure the complete result.** Use the workflow and methods the problem needs, including conventional automation. Count preparation, evaluation, and review as well as the task that became faster.
:::

Once a team identifies the work delaying its next decision, it needs a way to organize the study around it. A simulator result must remain tied to the workload and candidate it evaluated, and a failed check must guide the next design action. @sec-architecture-20-ontology develops that organization through six stages: Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit. Together they connect the architecture question to candidate development, evaluation, interpretation, and the decision about what to do next.
